ideas.name: 1. The first December Russell reconstitution (lists are already out): micro-cap deletions bought after the forced sale
ideas.rule: Leg B (the one I would run): at the close on Fri 11 Dec 2026, buy an equal-weight basket of the names on the final Russell 3000 and Russell Microcap deletion lists that leave the Russell family altogether (not takeovers, not names moving up), hedge with a short in IWM or IWC of equal dollar size, hold 20 sessions, exit about 12 Jan 2027. Leg A (optional, long-only plus hedge): from the close on Mon 16 Nov, hold the Russell 3000 additions that are not recent IPOs against IWM until the close on 11 Dec. Re-read the lists after each Friday update (20 Nov, 27 Nov, 4 Dec).
ideas.why_it_pays: Index funds must sell deletions at the 11 Dec close regardless of price. The deletions are, by construction, the stocks that ranked lowest on 30 Oct, so they are also the year's losers, and the forced sale lands in the middle of tax-loss season. Two price-insensitive sellers (index funds, then taxable holders) on the same names, followed by the January release of the second. The loser is the index fund's holders, who pay the reconstitution cost. Leg A is the well-known side and is likely crowded.
ideas.why_small: Names leaving the Russell Microcap are among the smallest listed stocks; positions of a few thousand dollars are all they take. The index-arbitrage desks trade the Russell 1000/2000 border, where the dollars are. The micro-cap tracker is small: IWC about $1.38bn at 24 Apr 2026 [S: etfcentral via search, not opened].
ideas.live_source: https://www.lseg.com/en/ftse-russell/russell-reconstitution lists four PDFs dated 13 Nov 2026, e.g. https://www.lseg.com/content/dam/ftse-russell/en_us/documents/other/rmicro-deletions-20261113.pdf (also rmicro-additions, ru3000-additions, ru3000-deletions, same pattern). I downloaded all four (HTTP 200) and parsed them: company, symbol, industry. Schedule from the LSEG release of 1 Sep 2026: rank day 30 Oct, lists 13 Nov, lockdown from 30 Nov, effective after the close 11 Dec [V].
ideas.history_source: There is no history for a December reconstitution: LSEG calls it the first in more than three decades [S: search summary of the LSEG insight page]. For June reconstitutions, CRSP daily on the desk's storage gives prices; membership has to be rebuilt, either from IWM and IWC holdings in the CRSP mutual-fund holdings tables the desk already pulled for the PCEF screen, or from market-cap rank on rank day. LSEG does not post old lists in one place that I found.
ideas.events_per_year: Counted from the 13 Nov 2026 PDFs [V]: Russell 3000 additions 127 (45 health care), Russell 3000 deletions 91 (39 health care), Microcap additions 112, Microcap deletions 150 (62 health care). 24 names are on both deletion lists (they leave the whole family); 47 are on both addition lists. With the June event this is now twice a year. The lists do not say why a name is deleted, so takeovers must be removed by hand or from EDGAR.
ideas.evidence: Dimensional, 2014 to 2023, 20 stocks a year per group, for stocks crossing the Russell 1000/2000 border only: deletions fell 1.1% in the 20 sessions before and recovered about 2% in the 20 after; additions rose 1.2% and gave back 0.95% [V: dimensional.com page read today]. That is the large end, not micro-caps. Onayev and Zdorovtsov (2007) report the effect weakened after 2002 [S]. Cai and Houge report deleted Russell 2000 stocks beat added ones by 67bp a month in the following year [S]. Research Affiliates (2025) finds large-index deletions outperform over 1990 to 2022 but not against the large indexes in the last decade [S]. I found nothing published on micro-cap deletions or on a December event. Carrion and Zhang (2024) find the tax-loss January effect has strengthened in muni closed-end funds [S], which supports the season, not this basket.
ideas.main_risk: One event, no December history: this is a single observation however it turns out. Deleted micro-caps are heavy in failing biotechs, so the basket's return will be dominated by a few names and by news, not by flow. Spreads are wide and closing auctions thin, so a paper fill at the quote overstates what a real auction would give. The short hedge in IWC may not be borrowable; IWM is a poorer match. Preliminary lists change in the three weekly updates.
ideas.first_test: On CRSP, June reconstitutions 2010 to 2025: rebuild the names that left IWC's holdings at each reconstitution, drop takeovers, and measure the 20-session return after the effective close against IWM, with a placebo date one month earlier (the placebo is what caught the YYY artifact in SCR-IDX-REBAL). In parallel, since the December event cannot be backtested, record the 24 double-deletion names and the wider deletion list as a shadow book from 11 Dec and report it as one observation.

ideas.name: 2. Leveraged single-stock funds on small underlyings: the forced close-of-day trade, bought back the next day
ideas.rule: Each day, for every leveraged single-stock ETF, compute the required rebalance in dollars as leverage x (leverage - 1) x fund net assets x the underlying's return that day (2 x AUM x r for a 2x fund), summed across all funds on the same stock, and divide by the stock's median closing-auction or daily dollar volume. When the stock is down on the day and the forced sale exceeds a threshold fixed in advance, buy the stock at that close and sell at the next close, hedged with IWM. The mirror (short after forced buying) needs borrow and is second priority.
ideas.why_it_pays: The fund must trade in the last minutes of the day in the direction of the day's move, in a size set by arithmetic, not by price. In a stock whose own close is thin, that pushes the closing price past fair value, and whoever takes the other side at the close is paid for it. The loser is the fund's holders, almost all retail: a Direxion-sponsored study reported by Reuters puts nearly 90% of trading in these funds with individuals [S: search result, not opened].
ideas.why_small: It only exists where the fund is large relative to the stock's closing volume, which means small and mid-cap underlyings; in TSLA or NVDA the flow is noise. The product class is new: more than 400 single-stock ETFs and over $31bn by mid-2026 according to secondary sites [S, sources inconsistent], so there is little history for anyone to have mined.
ideas.live_source: Issuer daily holdings files. Fetched: https://www.direxion.com/holdings/TSLL.csv returned HTTP 200, trade date 11/13/2026, shares outstanding 322,050,001, and each holding with shares, price and market value [V]. Direxion's list is mostly large underlyings; the small-underlying funds are at Tradr, Defiance, GraniteShares, Leverage Shares and T-Rex, and I did NOT confirm a machine-readable daily file for those (Defiance pages show a download button [S]). Fund prices and shares outstanding are also in any daily market data feed.
ideas.history_source: CRSP daily on the desk's storage carries ETFs with price and shares outstanding, which gives daily net assets for every such fund since the first US launches (July 2022 [U: recalled]) to 2025-12-31. Underlying returns and volume from the same file. No licensed closing-auction history is needed for a first pass.
ideas.events_per_year: Not counted. It depends on the threshold and on how many funds sit on small underlyings; that count is the first thing to make from CRSP. I would not quote a number before then.
ideas.evidence: Bessembinder (2025), Leveraged Single-Stock ETFs, measures the cost to fund holders: frictionless monthly returns fall short of the simple benchmark by 0.28% for 3x and 0.49% for -2x funds, attributed to daily rebalancing trades [S: search summary; the Alpha Architect page returned 403]. Jain, Mishra, Pagano and Rodriguez study index-level leveraged-ETF rebalancing and volatility [S]. I found no paper measuring the effect on the underlying stock's close for single-stock funds. That gap is the reason to look and also means there is no outside confirmation.
ideas.main_risk: Many of these funds hold swaps, and the swap dealer may hedge through the day or with options, so the trade may not arrive at the close at all. Big down days in small stocks carry news, and buying them is ordinary one-day reversal, which the desk found has earned nothing on the long side in small stocks since 2013 (st_reversal_small). The test must show the forced-flow measure adds something beyond the day's return. Shares outstanding lag by a day at some issuers.
ideas.first_test: From CRSP: list every single-stock leveraged ETF, compute daily required rebalance over underlying dollar volume, and count stock-days above 5% and 10%. If there are too few, stop. If not, regress next-day underlying return on the forced-flow ratio with the same-day return and its size as controls, and compare against matched stock-days with the same return and no leveraged fund (the control group). Separate the years before and after the product class grew.

ideas.name: 3. KBW high-yield index reconstitution (KBWY, KBWD): the December reshuffle of small REITs and lenders
ideas.rule: On the first session after KBW's Friday-evening rebalance release, buy the additions to the Premium Yield Equity REIT and Financial Sector Dividend Yield indexes at the close, hedged with VNQ or KBWY/KBWD respectively; sell at the close of the last session before the effective date (five sessions later). From that close, hold the deletions for ten sessions against the same hedge.
ideas.why_it_pays: Invesco's two funds must buy the additions and sell the deletions at the effective date. The indexes are yield-weighted and concentrated in a few dozen small REITs, mortgage REITs and business-development companies, so the highest-yielding (usually smallest, most beaten-down) additions get the biggest weights. The loser is the ETF holder, who buys after the run-up.
ideas.why_small: KBWY held about $325m at 17 Jul 2026 [S: Pensions & Investments via search]. A full position in one name is a few million dollars: meaningful against a small REIT's daily volume, irrelevant to an index-arbitrage desk.
ideas.live_source: KBW (Stifel) press release on GlobeNewswire, issued Friday evening. I read the Q4 2025 release in a syndicated copy (https://www.stockwatch.com/News/Item/U-z9600956-U!SF-20251212/U/SF): released 12 Dec 2025 20:30 ET, 'effective prior to the opening of business on Monday, December 22, 2025' [V]. The GlobeNewswire organisation RSS feed I tried returned 403, so a reliable machine feed is NOT yet confirmed; EDGAR does not carry these. A scraper of the Stifel newsroom or a news search on the fixed headline 'KBW Announces Index Rebalancing' is the fallback.
ideas.history_source: The same headline exists for every quarter back many years on newswire archives (Q4 2023, Q4 2024, 2025 quarters appeared in search [S]); the lists must be scraped into a file with a fetcher. Prices from CRSP. Fund weights from the CRSP mutual-fund holdings tables.
ideas.events_per_year: Q4 2025 release, counted [V]: Premium Yield Equity REIT 12 added, 9 deleted; Financial Sector Dividend Yield 8 added, 8 deleted; 37 additions and 34 deletions across six KBW indexes. Q1 2026 changed only the two bank indexes and Q1 2025 only dropped two REITs [S: search summaries], so nearly all the activity is in the December release: roughly 20 additions and 17 deletions a year in the two yield indexes, in one week.
ideas.evidence: None specific to these indexes that I found. General: Wang, Yao and Yelekenova, ETF Rebalancing, Hedge Fund Trades, and Capital Market, report stocks bought ahead of ETF rebalances outperform by 0.86% (t 3.86) before the rebalancing month and 0.75% during it [V: Quantpedia summary read today; sample period not given there]. The desk's own PCEF result is the closest relative: +184bp then -120bp, a post-hoc subgroup [S: results/IDEA_LEDGER.md].
ideas.main_risk: Additions are predictable from the public yield rule, so the move may happen before the release; the release-to-effective window may hold nothing. About 37 events a year in one week is one draw a year; a decade is ten draws. Yield-ranked deletions are often names that just cut dividends, so the deletion leg carries bad news as well as flow. The flow per name against its volume is not measured yet and may be under one day.
ideas.first_test: Size before returns: for the Dec 2025 lists, compute each addition's index weight x fund assets over its 20-day median dollar volume. If the median is under half a day, drop the idea. Otherwise scrape ten years of December releases and run the event study with a placebo window one month earlier and with the unchanged index members as the control group.

ideas.name: 4. S&P Select Industry equal-weight funds (XBI, KRE and siblings): the quarterly reset, predicted from the daily holdings file
ideas.rule: Ten sessions before each quarterly rebalance, read the fund's holdings file, compute each stock's gap between its current weight and its rule weight, convert to dollars with fund assets and to days of the stock's volume. Buy the ten names with the largest predicted purchase in days of volume, hedged with the fund itself, and sell at the rebalance close. Next 8 weeks: the December rebalance, expected Fri 18 Dec [U].
ideas.why_it_pays: An equal-weight fund must sell the quarter's winners and buy its losers back to target on one known day. In a fund of 150 small biotechs the bought names are the ones that fell most, where the fund's purchase is large against thin volume. The loser is the fund's holders, who pay the impact every quarter.
ideas.why_small: The stocks with the largest predicted purchase in days of volume are the smallest in the fund; the trade is capped by those names, not by the fund. Large desks do trade the big equal-weight rebalances; the small tail of sector funds like XPH, XSD, XES is less likely to be worth their while. I have no evidence on how crowded it is.
ideas.live_source: https://www.ssga.com/us/en/intermediary/library-content/products/fund-data/etfs/us/holdings-daily-us-en-xbi.xlsx (replace xbi with kre, xph, xsd): all four returned HTTP 200 with holdings as of 12-Nov-2026, columns Name, Ticker, Identifier, SEDOL, Weight, Sector, Shares Held [V]. XBI: 156 stocks, weights from 0.02% to 2.55%, median 0.46%. KRE: 167 stocks, 0.11% to 1.19%, median 0.48%. The file gives no fund assets; that comes from the fund page or price x shares outstanding.
ideas.history_source: SSGA does not publish past daily files, so archiving must start now. For a backtest: CRSP mutual-fund holdings on the desk's storage (period-end snapshots), or rebuild the rule weights from CRSP prices and the methodology. The methodology PDF (spglobal.com, methodology-sp-select-industry-indices.pdf) could not be opened today, so the rebalance date and the liquidity cap on weights are [U] and must be read before any code is written.
ideas.events_per_year: Four rebalances a year per fund. With ten names from each of roughly a dozen Select Industry funds [U: fund count not checked], a few hundred stock-events a year, clustered on four dates.
ideas.evidence: No study of these funds found. Same general evidence as idea 3 (Wang, Yao and Yelekenova [V via Quantpedia]). The weight spread I measured shows the reset is not small, but KRE's stepped weights (many names near 1.18%, a tail near 0.12%) show the liquidity cap matters: the target is not simply 1/N, and a naive prediction would be wrong for exactly the illiquid names the trade wants.
ideas.main_risk: It is short-term reversal in another form: the names bought are the quarter's losers, and the desk has found the long side of reversal weak in small stocks since 2013. The test has to beat a control of equally beaten-down stocks outside the fund. Biotech single-name news swamps flow. This is the same family as SCR-IDX-REBAL, where the pooled result was an artifact exposed by the placebo.
ideas.first_test: Read the methodology and reproduce the 18 Sep 2026 rebalance from two holdings snapshots in the CRSP fund-holdings tables: do predicted weight changes match actual share changes? If the prediction is good, run the event study on 2015 to 2025 with the outside-the-fund loser control and a placebo date mid-quarter.

ideas.name: 5. Dividend-streak indexes (SDY first): deletions known weeks before the index says so
ideas.rule: In the first week of January, list every member of the S&P High Yield Dividend Aristocrats index whose total dividend for the calendar year just ended did not exceed the prior year's (from CRSP distributions or EDGAR). These must be removed at the late-January reconstitution. After the forced sale at the effective date (about 1 Feb), buy them and hold 20 sessions against SDY. Additions (names reaching the required streak) can be held from the announcement to the effective date, long against SDY.
ideas.why_it_pays: Membership is a pure counting rule on public dividend history, so the changes are knowable before S&P publishes them. The index is weighted by yield, not size, so a small company can carry a weight far above its size and the fund's sale is large against its volume. The loser is the fund's holders.
ideas.why_small: Only a handful of names a year, and only the small ones matter. It is a January-only trade with a few positions; no desk builds a book around it.
ideas.live_source: NOT fetched. S&P's result notice exists (https://www.spglobal.com/spdji/en/documents/indexnews/announcements/20260123-1482009/1482009_hyda2026rebalanceannouncement.pdf) but returned 403 to me, as did the S&P blog. From search summaries only [S]: announced 23 Jan 2026, effective before the open 2 Feb 2026; 8 additions (THG, AFG, GL, STE, AMP, CMI, TRV, ACN), 2 deletions (UGI, JJSF). The pre-announcement list would be built by the desk itself from dividend records plus SDY's daily holdings file on ssga.com (same URL pattern as idea 4, verified for other tickers, not for SDY).
ideas.history_source: CRSP distributions on the desk's storage for dividend streaks; SDY holdings from the CRSP mutual-fund holdings tables for past membership; CRSP daily for prices.
ideas.events_per_year: About 10 in 2026 (8 in, 2 out) [S]; one S&P blog title reports 18 additions in 2024 [S: title only]. Too few to stand alone; it becomes a book only if the same rule is applied to the other streak indexes (NOBL in January; the Vanguard dividend-growth index and DVY in March [U: dates recalled]).
ideas.evidence: None found for this index. I did not find a study of dividend-streak index changes. Labelled speculative.
ideas.main_risk: Two deletions a year is not a sample. A company that stops raising its dividend has usually already fallen on that news, so the forced sale may be small against what has already happened, and S&P's exact test (fiscal against calendar year, treatment of specials) decides who is cut. The additions in 2026 were large companies where the fund's purchase is trivial.
ideas.first_test: From CRSP fund holdings, list every SDY entry and exit 2006 to 2025, and for each exit compute the fund's position over the stock's daily volume. If fewer than 30 exits exceed one day's volume, record it as too thin and stop. Only then look at returns.

scouts.not_proposed_and_why:
Plain micro-cap January effect (buy the year's losers in late December): not proposed on its own. I found no study after 2022 that tests it in US micro-caps; the only recent paper I found (Carrion and Zhang 2024 [S]) is about muni closed-end funds, which the desk has already covered. Idea 1's second leg is the dated, narrower version.
S&P SmallCap 600 additions and deletions, PCEF, PFF index additions, index-level leveraged-ETF close: already on results/IDEA_LEDGER.md as untested ideas.
Nasdaq Biotechnology Index December reconstitution (IBB): real and inside the eight weeks (company releases for 2025 cite effective 19 or 22 Dec 2025 [S, the two dates conflict]), but I could not find Nasdaq's official list or a count, so no live source is confirmed. Worth a follow-up, not a card.
Option-expiry pinning, buyback blackout windows, 13F window dressing: I did not find a free, timely event list or recent evidence in the time available; nothing to report beyond that.
Treasury month-end and auction effects in bond ETFs: already tested (month_end_ief on shadow, ust_auction_cycle not promoted).
Unverified items to treat with care: fund asset figures for KBWY and IWC are from search snippets and are months old; the S&P Select Industry rebalance date and cap rule, the 2026 KBW dates and the January 2027 S&P dates are inferred, not read; several pages (S&P, Alpha Architect, GlobeNewswire RSS) returned 403.

scouts.lane: Free alternative data from outside finance joined to US-listed small stocks (trade-remedy dockets, Medicare coverage, FDA device and drug calendars, trial registry, defence contracts)

ideas.name: 1. Trade-remedy calendar: buy the listed US petitioner around scheduled antidumping / countervailing-duty decisions
ideas.rule: For each new antidumping or countervailing-duty case where a petitioner (or a named domestic producer) is a US-listed stock under about $5bn, buy at the close after an affirmative USITC preliminary vote or an affirmative Commerce preliminary determination (the day importers must start posting cash deposits), hold 20 to 60 sessions, hedge with IWM or the sector ETF. Variant to test separately: enter 5 sessions before the scheduled vote date and exit at the close of the vote day. Long only; no borrow needed.
ideas.why_it_pays: A duty order raises the import price of the petitioner's exact product for five years or more, and the earnings effect arrives over the following quarters. The decisions are published in the Federal Register and on the USITC site, not on the newswires, and the affected companies are small industrial names with thin analyst coverage. The loser is the holder who sells or fails to buy because the news is a legal notice about 'lattice-boom crawler cranes' and not an earnings release. The dates are set by statute, so the calendar is known weeks ahead. Speculative on the drift: the published evidence is for the announcement window, not for what is left afterwards.
ideas.why_small: About 20 cases a year, each touching one to three listed names, many of them small caps (examples visible in the 2025-26 docket by product: crawler cranes, dissolving pulp, graphite electrodes, van-type trailers, railway tank cars, palladium). The petitioner-to-ticker link has to be read from the notice text by hand or by a parser. A large fund cannot build a book out of 20 small positions a year.
ideas.live_source: USITC Investigations Data System, https://ids.usitc.gov/investigations.json (no key). Fetched: HTTP 200, 37.3 MB, 4,446 investigation records with fields including Start Date, Vote Date, Commerce Preliminary AD/CVD Determination Date, Participants, HTS numbers [V]. It already lists scheduled future votes, for example Wooden Fence Components 2026-11-20, Seamless Pipe 2026-11-30, Railway Tank Cars 2026-12-03, Shopping Carts 2026-12-11 [V]. Second source for petitioner names and determinations: Federal Register API, https://www.federalregister.gov/api/v1/documents.json with conditions[agencies][]=international-trade-administration (fetched, returns titles and dates) and the public-inspection feed https://www.federalregister.gov/api/v1/public-inspection-documents/current.json (fetched, 108 documents, the first one an AD/CVD notice) which shows notices the business day before publication [V].
ideas.history_source: The same USITC file for dates back to the 1980s (preliminary-phase records are sparse before 2011 in this file: 1 to 3 a year in 2008-2010 against 12 or more from 2011, so treat 2011 onward as the usable sample [V]); Federal Register API for initiation notices and margins (full text from 1994); CRSP daily for returns. Petitioner names: the USITC file carries a 'Petitioner' participant type but it was empty on the 'Is Petitioner?' flag for every preliminary-phase record I checked [V], so names must come from the Federal Register initiation notice text or the petition itself. Not built.
ideas.events_per_year: Preliminary-phase AD/CVD investigations by start year, counted from the USITC file: 2019 16, 2020 25, 2021 14, 2022 7, 2023 12, 2024 27, 2025 20, 2026 to date 22 [V]. Federal Register notices whose title is 'Initiation of Less-Than-Fair-Value Investigation': 2019 14, 2022 8, 2024 25, 2025 22 [V]. Each case has three to four dated decisions. How many have a listed small-cap petitioner is NOT counted: the SEC ticker file refused my request, so no name match was run.
ideas.evidence: Blonigen, Tomlin and Wilson, NBER WP 9027 (2002), abstract read: affirmative US AD decisions are associated with '3% abnormal gains to a petitioning firm when there is no tariff-jumping FDI, but no abnormal gains if there is' [V]. Same paper's literature review: Hartigan, Kamma and Perry (1989) find significant effects only for threat-of-injury rulings; Mahdavi and Bhagwati (1994) find a negative reaction to the investigation itself in semiconductors [V, as reported in the paper]. A search summary reports a 2018 Forest Science study of furniture petitioners with mostly negative abnormal returns [S]. All samples are 1980s-1990s or single industries; nothing found on post-decision drift or on the post-2018 tariff era. Decay unknown.
ideas.main_risk: Filing a petition is itself a sign the business is hurting, so petitioners are a negatively selected group and a long book may just hold weak companies. Affirmative preliminary votes are the norm, so the surprise is small and may be fully priced on the day. Since 2025 broad tariffs change what an extra duty is worth. Matching petitioners to tickers is manual, and many petitioners are private or are large (steel majors).
ideas.first_test: Parse petitioner names from the 2011-2025 Federal Register initiation notices, match to CRSP names, and count how many cases have a listed petitioner under $5bn. If fewer than about 8 a year, stop. Otherwise compute market-adjusted returns from the close after each affirmative preliminary determination for 1, 5, 20 and 60 sessions, split 2011-2018 and 2019-2025, and compare with the same stocks on a date 120 sessions earlier.

ideas.name: 2. Medicare local coverage decisions: trade the small diagnostics or device company when its test appears in a proposed or final coverage policy
ideas.rule: Poll the CMS coverage database daily; when a new proposed or final local coverage determination names a product category sold by a listed small company (molecular tests, wound imaging, nerve ablation, cardiac monitors), buy at the next close if the policy grants coverage and hold 20 sessions against an IBB/XHE hedge; for a non-coverage draft, the mirror trade is a put or simply a block on holding the name. Second, dated leg: a final policy becomes effective on a stated later date, so test the window from posting to the effective date.
ideas.why_it_pays: For a single-product diagnostics company Medicare coverage is most of the revenue. The policies are posted on contractor pages and in a CMS database that almost no generalist reads; the company's own press release can come later or be worded softly. The loser is the holder who learns of the decision from the company's quarter-end report. The Castle Biosciences case shows the scale: a draft non-coverage policy in June 2023 was followed by a sharp fall, and the withdrawal of the draft in July 2023 by a rise of about 54% in a day; the January 2025 final decision cost 9% to 17% depending on the report [S: search summary of Motley Fool, Investing.com, The Fly; not opened]. Speculative: no study of this exists that I could find.
ideas.why_small: The affected companies are micro and small caps (single-test laboratories, small device makers). The link from a policy title to a ticker needs domain reading. A handful of events a year matter, each worth a small position.
ideas.live_source: CMS Coverage API, no key: https://api.coverage.cms.gov/v1/reports/local-coverage-proposed-lcds/ (fetched: HTTP 200, 102 rows, 45 distinct policy titles, each with contractor, updated_on date and comment-period end; newest row dated 10/30/2026) and https://api.coverage.cms.gov/v1/reports/local-coverage-final-lcds/ (fetched: HTTP 200, 935 rows with updated_on and effective_date; newest 11/06/2026 'MolDX: Predictive Classifiers for Early Stage Non-small Cell Lung Cancer', effective 11/12/2026) [V].
ideas.history_source: Weak. The API returns the current version of each policy with its last update date, not the first posting date of each past draft; of the 935 final rows, 437 carry a 2026 update date and 200 a 2025 date [V], which reflects revisions, not new policies. The Medicare Coverage Database has a downloadable archive that I did not fetch. A backtest would have to be built by hand from company 8-Ks (EDGAR full-text search for 'local coverage determination') joined to CRSP. No ready point-in-time history: say so.
ideas.events_per_year: Proposed policies currently listed: 45 distinct titles, of which roughly 28 were posted in 2026 and 15 in 2025 by my count of the listing [V]. Of the final list, 238 rows have molecular-test wording in the title [V]. The number that move a listed company is not counted; my guess is under 15 a year [U].
ideas.evidence: Only case evidence (Castle Biosciences 2023 and 2025, above) [S]. No paper found. Nothing to say about decay because nothing has been measured.
ideas.main_risk: The reaction may be complete within minutes of the posting, since specialist trade press (GenomeWeb, 360Dx) covers these the same day. Too few events to tell skill from luck. Mapping policy to ticker is judgement, which invites picking winners after the fact. The good-news side (coverage granted) may be the smaller move.
ideas.first_test: Use EDGAR full-text search for 8-Ks and press-release exhibits containing 'local coverage determination' since 2015, list the events by company, and measure the 1-day and 20-day market-adjusted return from the first public posting date. If the 20-day move after the first day is zero, the idea is only a risk flag for holdings, not a trade.

ideas.name: 3. Device clearances that appear in the FDA database before the company says anything
ideas.rule: Each time openFDA refreshes, list new 510(k) clearances, De Novo grants and original PMA approvals whose applicant matches a listed company under about $2bn; if the company has filed no 8-K or press release naming the clearance since the decision date, buy at the next close and hold 10 sessions or until the company announces, hedged with XHE or IWM. Long only.
ideas.why_it_pays: The clearance letter goes to the company on the decision date; the public database shows it at the next refresh. Small device companies often hold the news for a launch or a conference, and a 510(k) is not always treated as material enough for an 8-K. A reader of the database knows about a product approval the market has not been told about. The loser is the seller in those days. Speculative: the size of the reaction to small-company 510(k) news is not established in the literature.
ideas.why_small: Applicants are mostly private or foreign; the listed small-cap subset is a few hundred filings a year in illiquid names. Applicant names are subsidiaries and need a hand-kept map to tickers.
ideas.live_source: openFDA, no key: https://api.fda.gov/device/510k.json?sort=decision_date:desc and https://api.fda.gov/device/pma.json. Fetched: 176,625 510(k) records in total, meta.last_updated 2026-11-02, latest decision_date 2026-10-30 (so on 2026-11-15 the public file was about two weeks behind the calendar) [V]. Records carry applicant, decision_date, date_received, k_number, decision_code [V].
ideas.history_source: The same openFDA endpoints (510(k) history back to 1976 by FDA's description [S]) for decision dates; EDGAR 8-K full-text search and Alpaca/Benzinga news for the company's own announcement date; CRSP daily. The gap that matters: the file has the decision date but NOT the date each record first became public, so the backtest must assume a posting lag (test 7, 14 and 30 days) and the live book must record the true first-seen date from now on.
ideas.events_per_year: 2025: 3,225 510(k) decisions, of which 27 De Novo grants; 40 original PMA approvals [V, counted through the API]. More than 1,000 distinct applicants in 2025 (the count query caps at 1,000) [V]. The listed-small-cap share is not counted (no ticker match run); I would expect low hundreds [U].
ideas.evidence: Thin. A search summary reports an Aalborg University master's thesis finding short-window abnormal returns around FDA device approval announcements, a practitioner note on 35 AI-device clearances, and a single 2010 case of a 20% rise on 510(k) news [S, none opened]. No peer-reviewed study of the database-before-press-release gap was found.
ideas.main_risk: Most 510(k)s are routine line extensions worth nothing; the ones that matter are usually announced the same day by the company, leaving no gap. The posting lag is unknown historically, so a backtest can flatter itself by assuming the record was visible earlier than it was. Small device stocks have wide spreads.
ideas.first_test: For 2015-2025, match applicants to CRSP names, keep companies under $2bn, and for each clearance find the first 8-K or news item naming it. Report the share with no announcement within 5 sessions of the decision date, then the market-adjusted return from decision date + 14 calendar days over 10 sessions for that silent group against the announced group.

ideas.name: 4. Trial-registry edits: act on a sponsor's ClinicalTrials.gov status change before its press release
ideas.rule: Each morning pull industry-sponsored studies whose record was posted as updated the previous day; flag a change to Terminated, Suspended or Withdrawn, or a primary-completion date pushed out by more than 6 months, where the lead sponsor is a listed company under about $2bn and the study is its Phase 2 or 3 lead programme. Use as (a) a block list for the desk's small-cap long books (earnings drift, follow-ons, converts hold many biotechs) and (b) a put-buying or short signal where borrow exists, held 20 sessions.
ideas.why_it_pays: Sponsors are legally required to update the registry within set windows, and the registry team often does so before investor relations says anything. The record I pulled shows the mechanism: Ultragenyx study NCT07157254 was submitted as 'Terminated: Lack of efficacy' on 2026-10-30 and posted publicly on 2026-11-03 [V]. The loser is the holder who waits for the press release. The value to this desk is mostly avoiding losses on longs it already holds, which needs no borrow.
ideas.why_small: The signal is on the short side in small biotechs where borrow is scarce and options are thin, so it does not scale. Sponsor-to-ticker matching and deciding whether a study is material to the company need a maintained map.
ideas.live_source: ClinicalTrials.gov API v2, no key: https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies with filter.overallStatus=TERMINATED,SUSPENDED,WITHDRAWN and query.term=AREA[LeadSponsorClass]INDUSTRY AND AREA[LastUpdatePostDate]RANGE[from,to]. Fetched: 182 such studies posted between 2026-10-15 and 2026-11-15, with sponsor name, status, whyStopped text, lastUpdateSubmitDate and lastUpdatePostDate; API data timestamp 2026-11-13 [V].
ideas.history_source: Not confirmed. The API returns only the current version of each record. The per-study change history exists on the website, but the internal history endpoint returned 403 to my request, and the AACT archive download page returned 404 [V]. Without dated past versions a backtest can only use each stopped study's last update date, which is biased. A proper history source (AACT monthly snapshots or the site's record-history pages) must be confirmed before any return is quoted.
ideas.events_per_year: 1,617 industry-sponsored studies currently in a stopped status had their last update posted during 2025 [V]; this counts last updates, not the status-change date, and includes large pharma and private sponsors. The listed-small-cap, lead-programme subset is not counted.
ideas.evidence: Vendor article (AppliedXL, read): cites a 2022 PLOS ONE study of 13,807 trials with returns of -9.3% for suspensions, -9.6% for enrollment holds and -11.7% for delays, and gives cases such as an enrollment shortfall visible 83 days before a -49% disclosure; its own backtests are described only as 'directional correlations' on 'a limited dataset' [V that the article says this; the PLOS figures themselves are S, the paper page would not load]. Rothenstein et al., JNCI 2011, 59 oncology Phase 3 announcements 2000-2009: prices rose 13.7% over the 120 days before positive results (95% CI -2.2% to 29.6%) and fell 0.7% before negative ones [S]. At least one vendor sells this signal, so the easy cases are probably watched.
ideas.main_risk: Most terminations are of minor studies or were already announced; the registry often lags the press release, not the other way round. No confirmed point-in-time history, so no honest backtest yet. As a short it fails on borrow at Alpaca, as reverse splits did.
ideas.first_test: Confirm a dated-version source first. Then, for 2018-2025, take status changes to Terminated or Suspended for sponsors matched to CRSP under $2bn, find the first 8-K or news item on the programme, and report (a) the share where the registry came first and (b) the market-adjusted return from the registry posting date to 20 sessions later. Separately count how many names the small-cap earnings-drift book would have held on those dates.

ideas.name: 5. Defence contract awards that are large against the winner's market value
ideas.rule: After the 5pm ET daily Department of War contract list, match awardees to listed companies; if the award value is above 5% of market capitalisation (new award, not a modification or a multi-vendor ceiling) and the company is under about $2bn, buy at the next close, hold 20 sessions, hedge with IWM or ITA. Long only.
ideas.why_it_pays: The list is published after the close in a block of text naming dozens of awardees; small winners often issue no press release for days, and the amount is not scaled to company size anywhere. A contract worth a tenth of market value is a real change in backlog. The loser is the seller the next morning who has not read the list.
ideas.why_small: Only awards that are large relative to a small company matter, which limits the trade to small names; primes are fully covered by analysts. Awardee names are subsidiaries and need mapping.
ideas.live_source: RSS feed https://www.war.gov/DesktopModules/ArticleCS/RSS.ashx?ContentType=400&Site=945&max=10 (fetched with a browser user-agent: HTTP 200, ten daily items, the latest 'contracts-for-nov-13-2026' stamped Fri 13 Nov 2026 22:02 GMT, i.e. just after 5pm ET; feed text says contracts 'valued at $7.5 million or more') [V]. The article pages themselves returned 403 to plain requests, so the award text was NOT read here; a browser-like client would be needed. Cross-check and amounts: USAspending API, POST https://api.usaspending.gov/api/v2/search/spending_by_award/ (fetched, no key, returns recipient, amount, start date, last-modified time) [V]; published guidance says Defence records reach it with a delay of about 90 days [U], so it is for history, not for the live trigger.
ideas.history_source: USAspending bulk and API (search limited to 2007-10-01 onward per the API's own message [V]) for award date, amount and recipient; the dated daily announcement archive on war.gov for the public time; CRSP for returns and market value. Recipient-to-ticker by name with a hand-kept subsidiary table.
ideas.events_per_year: About 250 daily lists a year (ten lists in the ten business days to 2026-11-13 [V]). The number of awards per list and the number above 5% of a small company's value were not counted because the article pages were blocked; expect a few dozen qualifying events a year [U].
ideas.evidence: A search summary reports: Palkar, Larson and Larson (Applied Financial Economics 2012) find positive announcement-day abnormal returns for military contract awards and examine days -1 to +60; a CESifo working paper (no. 7534) on US federal procurement finds winners earn abnormal returns with no sign of anticipation; Diltz (1990) finds some positive effect [S, none opened]. None isolates small firms or sizes the award against market value. Retail data vendors now publish contract feeds, so the announcement-day move is likely contested; the drift is untested.
ideas.main_risk: Headline values are ceilings on multi-year, multi-vendor vehicles and overstate what one firm gets. Many awards are expected follow-ons. The live page blocks simple clients. Small defence names can gap at the open, so a next-close entry may get nothing.
ideas.first_test: From USAspending 2008-2025, take new definitive contracts and delivery orders of $7.5m or more to recipients matched to CRSP companies under $2bn, compute award over market value, and report market-adjusted returns from the close after the award date over 1, 5 and 20 sessions by size bucket, split 2008-2016 and 2017-2025. Check a sample of 30 against the daily list for the true public date.

ideas.name: 6. The run-up into a dated FDA decision, exited before the decision
ideas.rule: Collect each small company's stated FDA target action date from its own 8-K text; buy 30 sessions before the date and sell 3 sessions before it, never holding through the decision; hedge with XBI. Long only.
ideas.why_it_pays: Holders who want the binary outcome buy ahead of it and those who do not want it cannot short easily, so prices tend to rise into the date; the exit before the decision gives up the outcome and keeps the anticipation. The loser is the late buyer of the lottery ticket. This is widely known among retail biotech traders, which is the main reason it ranks last.
ideas.why_small: The names are small and volatile and a book holds a handful at a time; position size is limited by the gap risk if the agency acts early.
ideas.live_source: EDGAR full-text search, https://efts.sec.gov/LATEST/search-index?q="PDUFA target action date"&forms=8-K&dateRange=custom&startdt=...&enddt=... (fetched: 33 8-K filings in 2026-10-15 to 2026-11-15, for example Praxis, Atara, Palvella, CorMedix, uniQure) [V]. The date itself must be parsed from the filing text. FDA publishes no list of these dates.
ideas.history_source: EDGAR full-text search back to 2001 for the dates; CRSP daily for returns. Same search for the whole of 2025 with the single word 'PDUFA' returned 346 8-K filings, concentrated in repeat filers (one company 27 times) [V], so distinct decision dates are far fewer than filings.
ideas.events_per_year: 346 8-K filings mentioning the term in 2025 [V]; distinct decision dates not counted, probably 60 to 100 [U].
ideas.evidence: Rothenstein et al., JNCI 2011 (Phase 3 oncology announcements 2000-2009): +13.7% over the 120 days before positive results with a confidence interval that includes zero [S]. A 2000 study reported via search: +27% for eventual winners against -4% for losers from 120 to 3 days before Phase 3 results [S]. Both condition on the outcome, so neither shows an unconditional run-up. A vendor (BiopharmaWatch) says about 1 in 5 approved stocks had risen 20% or more in the 90 sessions before the decision and that about 6 in 10 recent approvals came before the stated date [S, methodology unpublished]. No unconditional, recent, peer-reviewed estimate found; assume it has weakened.
ideas.main_risk: Early decisions: if most approvals arrive before the date, an exit 3 sessions ahead still holds through many outcomes. Small biotechs issue shares into strength, which the desk's follow-on work already measures. The effect may be XBI beta.
ideas.first_test: Parse target dates from 8-Ks for 2012-2025, compute XBI-adjusted returns for sessions -30 to -3 for all events regardless of outcome, split by half, and report the share of events where the decision came before session -3.

scouts.not_proposed_and_why:
Nothing was backtested: these are six scouting cards, and no return figure in them is mine. Before starting I read the titles and status lines of all 19 cards in `results/ideas/`, the free-data inventory in `results/events/PREDICTION_MARKETS_ALT_DATA_2026-10-15.md`, and the ledger; none of the outside-finance sources in this lane had been touched.

Gaps that apply across the cards:
- **No ticker matching was run.** The SEC ticker file refused my request without a contact address, which I did not supply. Every "listed small-cap subset" count is therefore missing or marked [U].
- **Papers not opened.** The NBER antidumping paper is the only one I read directly. The PLOS ONE trial-outcome paper sat behind a browser check; its figures are second-hand.
- **Idea 4 has no confirmed point-in-time history.** The trial-registry history endpoint returned 403 and the archive page 404.
- **Idea 5's award text was not read.** The daily contract pages returned 403; only the RSS feed listing them was fetched.

Considered and left out:
- **Congressional trade disclosures and lobbying:** already packaged in ETFs and vendor feeds; filing lag of up to 45 days; not niche.
- **FDA warning letters, import alerts, NHTSA recalls, CFPB complaints, OSHA, EPA:** bad-news signals that need a short. The reverse-split card already found Alpaca will not lend such names. Recalls and complaints mostly hit large companies.
- **PTAB decisions and court dockets:** the outcome is priced on the day. The free docket mirror is not real-time, and the USPTO data portal needs a registered key, which I did not use.
- **USITC Section 337 import-ban cases:** the same file as idea 1 carries them, 43 started in 2025 and 56 in 2026 to date, nearly all with a target date [V]. Most involve large technology companies; worth a look only as an extension if idea 1 survives.
- **Medicare payment rules on the Federal Register public-inspection feed:** the feed works [V], but there are about a dozen rules a year and prices react immediately.
- **Wikipedia page views, Google Trends, app ranks, job postings, web traffic, ship tracking:** either no free dated history or only weak evidence; the earlier repo note already rated page views as weak.
- **Weather, power prices, commodity-linked small caps:** the commodity itself is priced in futures the desk cannot trade, and I found no dated event to trade on.
- **Grant awards (SBIR, NIH, DOE):** small against company value and announced by the companies themselves; not probed.

scouts.lane: Free alternative data from regulatory filings and public registries, joined to small stocks. Long-only or long-vs-ETF ideas only; the short-side filing flags were already censused by the desk and died on borrow.

ideas.name: 1. Thrift mutual-to-stock conversions: hold the first year, leave before the second
ideas.rule: When a savings institution completes a standard or second-step mutual-to-stock conversion and its shares start trading on Nasdaq or NYSE, buy at the close of the fifth trading day, hedge with a regional-bank ETF (KRE), and sell at the close of trading day 250. A second, separate leg to test is long from month 30 to month 42, around the date the takeover restriction lapses.
ideas.why_it_pays: Buyers in the offering also receive the pre-conversion capital for free, so the shares start well below tangible book. Regulation then fixes a calendar: the company may not repurchase shares in the first year (12 CFR 239.63(c)(1) [V: ecfr.gov, fetched 2026-11-15]), may adopt a stock plan only after six months (239.63(a)(1)(vi) [V]), and nobody may acquire more than 10% for a set period after conversion (239.63(f)(1) [V for the 10% bar; the three-year term is [S], the fetch did not quote the duration]). The other side is the depositor who subscribed for the first-day gain and sells, and local holders with no view on price to book.
ideas.why_small: Typical deals raise tens of millions of dollars and trade thinly; three to twelve a year. A fund cannot build a position, and the specialist bank funds that do this mostly get their shares as depositors in the offering, not in the after-market.
ideas.live_source: EDGAR full-text search, https://efts.sec.gov/LATEST/search-index?q="plan of conversion" "subscription offering" "community offering"&dateRange=custom&category=custom&forms=424B3,S-1&startdt=YYYY-MM-DD&enddt=YYYY-MM-DD . Fetched 2026-11-15: HTTP 200; for 2026 to date it returned 14 424B3 documents from 6 issuers (CSB Financial, Columbia Financial, MFB Bancorp, PSB Financial, Rhinebeck Bancorp, URSB Bancorp) [V]. The S-1 arrives months before trading starts, so there is ample notice. The first trading day itself must come from the issuer's 8-K or a new symbol in Alpaca's asset list (not checked here).
ideas.history_source: SDC new issues on the desk's storage (IPOs with SIC 6035/6036) joined to CRSP daily for first trading dates and returns; EDGAR 424B3 text for standard versus second-step and the pro-forma price to book. EDGAR full-text search only reaches back to about 2001 [U], so the 1990s wave needs SDC and CRSP.
ideas.events_per_year: Distinct issuers with a matching 424B3, counted now from EDGAR full-text search [V]: 2015: 8; 2017: 6; 2019: 7; 2021: 12; 2022: 3; 2023: 7; 2024: 5; 2025: 6; 2026 to 15 Nov: 6. Roughly half of the recent ones show an exchange ticker in EDGAR (AVBC, HYNE, SNNF, MFDB, RBKB); the rest appear to be OTC and not tradable at Alpaca [U: exchange not verified per name].
ideas.evidence: Friesen and Swift, 'Overreaction in the thrift IPO aftermarket', Journal of Banking & Finance 33(7), 2009 [V: abstract read on RePEc 2026-11-15]: with the first-day return removed, cumulative excess returns stay positive for 12 months; a correction starts in year two, lasts about 18 months and is strongest in small thrifts. The abstract gives no magnitudes or sample dates, so those are a stated gap. Brewer, Evanoff and So (Chicago Fed working paper, 1985-96 sample) link insider subscriptions to better after-market performance [S]. No post-2009 replication found; decay unknown.
ideas.main_risk: Small sample (about 5 to 10 a year, fewer once OTC names are removed), so one test cannot say much; the year-one return may be bank-sector beta and value, which the KRE hedge only partly removes; spreads are wide and a $1M book would be a large share of daily volume. The paper's sample is the 1990s-2000s conversion wave and the effect may be gone.
ideas.first_test: From SDC and CRSP, list every thrift conversion IPO 2000-2025 that listed on an exchange; compute day-5 to day-250 return less KRE (and less a matched small-bank basket) by era, then the same for months 13-30 as the control the paper says should be negative. Report median daily dollar volume in the first year before anything else.

ideas.name: 2. Insiders buying in their own company's registered offering
ideas.rule: When a company prices a follow-on or registered direct offering and, within three business days, one or more officers or directors file a Form 4 with an open-market or offering purchase (code P) at the offer price, buy at the next close and hold 20 sessions against IWM; the control is the same trade on offerings with no insider purchase.
ideas.why_it_pays: The desk's own follow-on card found the post-pricing recovery was real and has faded to 0.26 since 2013 [S: results/ideas/2026-11-15_follow_ons.md]. An officer who pays the same price as the buyers, in cash, at the moment of maximum dilution separates financings that fund something from financings of last resort. The other side is the holder who sells every offering alike, and funds that bought the deal to flip it.
ideas.why_small: About 30 to 50 issuers a year flag insider interest in the prospectus, mostly small biotech and other sub-$500M companies; the join between a prospectus and a Form 4 two days later is fiddly and no vendor sells it as a signal.
ideas.live_source: Two EDGAR feeds. (a) Prospectus text: https://efts.sec.gov/LATEST/search-index?q="indicated an interest in purchasing" "directors" "officers"&dateRange=custom&category=custom&forms=424B5&startdt=...&enddt=... , fetched 2026-11-15, HTTP 200, 50 documents from 32 issuers for 2025 and 71 from 47 for 2019 [V]. (b) Form 4 as filed: https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcurrent&type=4&output=atom (the same endpoint was fetched for SCHEDULE 13D and returned 40 entries stamped to 2026-11-13 21:46 ET [V]; the type=4 variant was not fetched). A Form 4 is due within two business days, so the entry is one to three sessions after pricing.
ideas.history_source: SDC new issues on the desk's storage (already staged by scripts/research/stage_sdc_follow_ons.py) joined to the SEC Insider Transactions Data Sets, quarterly zips listed at https://www.sec.gov/data-research/sec-markets-data/insider-transactions-data-sets (page fetched 2026-11-15; the latest file listed is 2026q3_form345.zip [V]), which the desk already used for its cluster census; CRSP daily for returns.
ideas.events_per_year: 32 issuers in 2025 and 47 in 2019 whose 424B5 states that directors or officers indicated an interest in buying [V: counted now]. The number with an actual code-P Form 4 at the offer price has not been counted and is the first thing to measure; 424B4 and S-1 deals are not in this count.
ideas.evidence: No study of this exact conditioning was found in three searches; this is a labelled speculation. Adjacent: Wilson Sonsini's PIPE and registered-direct report says insider participation was 18.5% of deals in 2024 against 27.6% in 2023 [S: wsgr.com report, not opened]; Clarke, Dunbar and Kahle (JFQA 2001) tie pre-filing insider trading to post-offering performance [S]. The desk's own result that plain follow-on recovery faded after 2013 is the base rate.
ideas.main_risk: Many 'insiders' in these deals are venture funds with a board seat, not individuals, and their participation can be a condition of the deal getting done, which is a weak-company marker. Issuers are biotech-heavy, so results may be one sector's beta. The Form 4 can arrive after the bounce. The control (offerings without insider purchases) may do as well, which is this desk's second most common cause of death.
ideas.first_test: Join the staged SDC follow-ons to the SEC Form 4 purchase rows by issuer CIK and date (transaction date within 0 to 3 business days of pricing, price within 2% of the offer price). Count events a year, split individuals from funds, then run the existing follow_ons explore harness with the flag on and off, entering at the close after the Form 4's acceptance time.

ideas.name: 3. First Schedule 13D on a micro-cap with a stated activist purpose, read from the structured XML
ideas.rule: Each evening read new initial Schedule 13D filings; keep those where the issuer is an exchange-listed operating company below the 2,000th by size, the filer is not an officer, director or pre-IPO holder, the funds source is working capital or personal funds, and Item 4 states a plan (board seats, sale, strategic review); buy at the next close and hold 40 sessions against IWM.
ideas.why_it_pays: A 13D with a plan is a dated statement that someone with capital intends to change the company. In a micro-cap nobody covers, the filing is often the only announcement. The other side is holders who do not read EDGAR and sellers who supplied the filer's block. The 2024 rule change cut the filing deadline from ten calendar days to five business days [S: law-firm summaries of SEC release 33-11253, Oct 2023], so less of the move can happen before the filing than in the published samples.
ideas.why_small: The published work is on hedge-fund campaigns at companies large enough to matter to funds. Below about $300M of market value the filers are individuals, family offices and small partnerships, and the position a follower can take is a few tens of thousands of dollars.
ideas.live_source: https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcurrent&type=SCHEDULE%2013D&owner=include&count=40&output=atom , fetched 2026-11-15: HTTP 200, 40 entries, newest accepted 2026-11-13 21:46 ET [V]. Each filing has primary_doc.xml with machine-readable fields; the one opened (Pyxus International, accepted 2026-11-13 17:00:20) carried dateOfEvent, issuerCusipNumber, percentOfClass, fundType, typeOfReportingPerson and the Item 4 text under transactionPurpose [V]. That example is a debt-exchange holder, not an activist, which shows why the Item 4 filter is needed.
ideas.history_source: EDGAR quarterly form indexes (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/full-index/YYYY/QTRn/form.gz, fetched for all four 2025 quarters [V]) for every SC 13D / SCHEDULE 13D since 1994 with acceptance times from the filing headers; Item 4 is free text before 2024-12-18, so the history needs a text classifier or the desk's event-extraction engine; CRSP daily for returns. The desk's card says 'following activist 13Ds' is dead: that entry sits in the closed-end-fund list of results/events/SS_DESK_EXPANSION_2026-10-19.md and I found no test on operating companies; confirm before spending time.
ideas.events_per_year: 1,115 initial Schedule 13D filings in 2025 (distinct accession numbers in the EDGAR form index, counted now [V]); 4,522 amendments. The share that are exchange-listed micro-cap operating companies with an activist Item 4 is not counted; a plausible range cannot be given without reading them, so it is a stated gap.
ideas.evidence: Brav, Jiang, Partnoy and Thomas (2008), hedge-fund 13Ds 2001-06: about 7 to 8% abnormal return over days -20 to +20 and no reversal over the next year [S: search summary of the paper]. Klein and Zur (2006/2008): 10.2% around the filing for hedge-fund targets, 5.1% for other activists, not reversed in a year [S]. Karpouzis et al. (2023): post-filing returns exist but are well below the pre-filing run-up [S]. None reports a micro-cap subsample, and how much is left after a next-close entry is exactly what is unknown.
ideas.main_risk: Most of the published return is before and on the filing day; 72% of filings of this kind land after 16:00 ET on the desk's earlier censuses, so the first reaction is at the next open, before a close fill. The same names are small, beaten-down value stocks, so a losers control must be run alongside. Classifying Item 4 on the pre-2024 history is where a lookahead or selection error would creep in.
ideas.first_test: On the structured filings only (2024-12-18 to today, about 1,100 a year), apply the mechanical filters, count what is left, and measure the return from the first close after acceptance to +1, +5, +20 and +40 sessions against IWM and against a matched loser. If fewer than 50 events a year survive or the +1 to +40 return is inside the control, stop before building the text classifier.

ideas.name: 4. Dilution-armed flag as a filter on the small-stock earnings-drift longs
ideas.rule: In the existing pead_small long book, drop any name that has filed an at-the-market prospectus supplement (424B5 naming a sales agent) or had a shelf go effective in the prior 90 days and whose last 10-K or 10-Q carries going-concern language; nothing is shorted.
ideas.why_it_pays: A small company with an open at-the-market programme sells stock into exactly the strength a good earnings surprise creates, so the drift the book is trying to earn is capped by the issuer. The other side of the unfiltered trade is the company itself. This is a filter on a book the desk already found (1.27 gross as fixed, about 0.7 on a free feed [S: results/ideas/2026-11-15_pead_small.md]), not a new sleeve.
ideas.why_small: It only matters below the size where at-the-market sales are a meaningful share of volume; in large stocks the flag is irrelevant.
ideas.live_source: EDGAR daily and quarterly form indexes, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/full-index/2025/QTR1/form.gz and siblings, fetched 2026-11-15 [V]; the at-the-market wording can be confirmed per filing through the full-text search endpoint used above (fetched, HTTP 200 [V]).
ideas.history_source: EDGAR form indexes for 424B5 and S-3 effectiveness since 2008, full-text search for the sales-agreement wording from 2001 [U on start year], and the SEC financial-statement data sets for going-concern text; joined by CIK to the pead_small panel on CRSP and IBES.
ideas.events_per_year: 3,388 distinct 424B5 filings in 2025 across all issuers (EDGAR form index, counted now [V]). How many are at-the-market programmes at companies inside the pead_small universe has not been counted.
ideas.evidence: Billett, Floros and Garfinkel, 'At-the-Market Offerings', JFQA 54(3), 2019: at-the-market programmes became possible in 2008 and by 2016 their count was 63% of seasoned offerings; users are smaller, more opaque firms [S: RePEc abstract summary]. I found no paper measuring returns after an at-the-market filing, so the return effect is a labelled speculation; the desk's own A1 closed-end-fund issuance gate failed at zero trials [S: docs/RESEARCH_STATE.md].
ideas.main_risk: The flag may simply mark small, cash-burning companies, which the earnings-surprise sort already tilts away from, in which case it removes nothing. Sales under a programme are disclosed in arrears, so an open programme is not the same as active selling.

ideas.name: 5. Civilian federal contract awards that are large against a micro-cap's size, read from the registry
ideas.rule: Each evening pull new federal contract awards from USAspending for civilian agencies; where the recipient maps to an exchange-listed company and the obligated amount is at least 10% of market value, and the company has filed no 8-K or press release on it, buy at the next close and hold 20 sessions against IWM.
ideas.why_it_pays: Civilian contract actions reach the public procurement registry within days, and a micro-cap often announces late or not at all. The other side is holders who learn of the award only from the next earnings report. Speculative: the published work says the price effect sits on the announcement day, so the trade works only where the registry is ahead of the announcement.
ideas.why_small: Mapping recipient names and subsidiaries to tickers is manual and unlicensed; awards that are large relative to a $50M company are small in dollars and of no interest to a fund that follows prime contractors.
ideas.live_source: POST https://api.usaspending.gov/api/v2/search/spending_by_award/ with a time_period filter and award_type_codes A-D. Fetched 2026-11-15: HTTP 200, results with Last Modified Date values from 2026-11-03 to 2026-11-12 [V]. Two limits found: the search endpoint only reaches back to 2007-10-01, with bulk downloads to 2000-10-01 [V: API message]; and Defense Department records are withheld from public view for 90 days after signing [S: fpds.gov data-availability page and DFARS PGI 204.6, via search], so this is a civilian-agency idea. The Defense Department's daily announcement page (defense.gov/News/Contracts and war.gov/News/Contracts) returned HTTP 403 to both fetches, so I could not confirm it as a live source.
ideas.history_source: USAspending bulk award archives (2000-10-01 onward) for awards; CRSP for prices and market value; EDGAR company names and Exhibit 21 subsidiary lists for the recipient-to-ticker map. The date an award first became publicly visible is not the action date; whether the archive preserves a first-publication date is unverified [U], and without it the backtest has lookahead.
ideas.events_per_year: Not counted. The count needs the recipient-to-ticker map, which does not exist yet; this is a stated gap, not an estimate.
ideas.evidence: Gomez Cram, Guo, Kung and Mecca, 'Government Spending and Rising Industry Stars', CEPR DP 20454, March 2025: firms with positive procurement shocks earn large abnormal returns, concentrated on the few days of award announcements [S: abstract summary]. A 2026 Bank of Lithuania working paper on Defense award announcements finds no reliable post-award pattern [S]. Diltz (1990) and Palkar, Larson and Larson (Applied Financial Economics 2012) find positive announcement-day returns [S]. Nothing found on drift or on micro-caps.
ideas.main_risk: The registry date may lag the company's own announcement rather than lead it; modifications and option exercises on old contracts look like new awards; indefinite-delivery ceilings overstate what will be spent; the name map will have errors that look like signal.
ideas.first_test: Before any returns: take 50 recent civilian awards to listed micro-caps by hand, and for each compare the registry's first-visible date with the first 8-K or press release. If the registry is not ahead in at least half, the idea is closed at no cost.

ideas.name: 6. Late filers that cure: long when the delinquent report is finally filed
ideas.rule: For a company that filed a late-filing notice and missed the grace period, buy at the close after it files the overdue 10-K or 10-Q, or files an 8-K saying it regained compliance with the exchange's periodic-filing rule, and hold 20 sessions against IWM; exclude bid-price cures.
ideas.why_it_pays: The desk censused the late-filing notice as a short and killed it on borrow (30.4% of 2025 filers shortable [S: SS_DESK_EXPANSION_2026-10-19.md, D4]). The cure is the long-only mirror: the delisting threat ends and holders barred from delinquent issuers can return. The other side is whoever sold during the delinquency because they had to. Speculative: I found no study of returns at the cure.
ideas.why_small: About 30 to 40 issuers a year, nearly all micro-caps recovering from an accounting problem; too few and too small for a fund, and no vendor flags the cure.
ideas.live_source: EDGAR full-text search: https://efts.sec.gov/LATEST/search-index?q="regained compliance" "5250(c)(1)"&dateRange=custom&category=custom&forms=8-K&startdt=...&enddt=... , fetched 2026-11-15, HTTP 200 [V]. The overdue report itself appears in the EDGAR current-filings feed (same endpoint as idea 3 with type=10-K or 10-Q; that variant not fetched).
ideas.history_source: EDGAR form indexes: every NT 10-K and NT 10-Q since 1994 with the date the matching report was finally filed (the desk's census already holds 63,125 notices for 2008-25 [S]); 8-K Item 3.01 text for exchange notices; CRSP daily.
ideas.events_per_year: 8-Ks containing 'regained compliance' and Nasdaq rule 5250(c)(1): 33 issuers in 2025, 38 in 2024; the NYSE equivalent (802.01E) returned 1 in 2025 [V: counted now]. For scale, bid-price cures (rule 5550(a)(2)) were 210 issuers in 2025 [V] and are excluded because most are reverse splits. Late notices themselves: 732 NT 10-K and 1,150 NT 10-Q in 2025 [V: form index].
ideas.evidence: Bartov and Konchitchki (Accounting Horizons, 2,115 first-time late filers): five-day returns of -2.93% for NT 10-Q and -1.96% for NT 10-K, continued downward drift, worse for those that miss the grace period [S: press summaries of the paper]. That is evidence on the notice, not the cure; nothing on the cure was found.
ideas.main_risk: The cure may be fully priced on the day (the 8-K is usually after the report is filed, so the news is already out); survivors that cure are selected on having recovered, and the 20 sessions after may just be small-stock rebound; 30-odd events a year gives little power.
ideas.first_test: From the form indexes, pair every NT notice 2008-2025 with the date the overdue report arrived, keep those more than 15 days late on listed stocks, and measure +1 to +20 sessions after the filing against IWM and against the same stocks 60 sessions later.

scouts.lane: Obscure corporate-action plumbing in US-listed small and micro caps (wind-downs, cash-outs, conversions, squeeze-outs). All work read-only; nothing in the repo was changed. Tags: [V] fetched and read on 2026-11-15, [S] a source or search summary says so but the primary was not opened, [U] uncertain.
