ideas.name: 1. Reverse/forward split cash-outs (going-private 'odd-lot' stubs): buy just under the cash-out threshold
ideas.rule: Event: an exchange-listed issuer files a Schedule 13E-3 (or preliminary proxy) for a reverse split immediately followed by a forward split, in which holders of fewer than N shares are paid a fixed cash price. Enter at the next close after the filing if price is below the cash-out price by more than a set margin, buying at most N-1 shares. Exit: the mandatory cash payment on the effective date (no election is needed), or sell at market if the board abandons the plan. Long only, no hedge (position is a fixed cash claim).
ideas.why_it_pays: The cash price is fixed for small holders only. Holders above the threshold cannot get it, so the usual arbitrage capital has no way in; the remaining gap is paid by small holders who sell early to avoid waiting for a delisting. Loser: retail sellers between announcement and effective date. Example: Tile Shop (Nasdaq: TTSH) announced on 2025-10-06/07 a cash-out at $6.60 for holders under the ratio; shares went to $6.42 after hours, an 11.7% premium to the prior close was stated [S: Reuters summary via search]. The split took effect 2025-12-15 at 1-for-3,000 and the company paid about $32.2m for 4,875,290 shares [S: 10-K via search; ratio and $6.60 V: 8-K exhibit 99.1 dated 2025-12-03]. That is roughly 2.8% gross over about ten weeks on at most 2,999 shares (about $19.8k), by my arithmetic from those two prices.
ideas.why_small: The position is capped by the threshold: under 3,000 shares at Tile Shop, under 400 at Cyanotech [V], 2,500 to 7,500 at Anebulo [S]. A fund cannot put more than a few thousand to a few tens of thousands of dollars into one event per account. The catalogue closed this as G2 on capacity on 2026-10-15; the team lead's 2026-11-15 ruling that small capacity is fine is what reopens it.
ideas.live_source: EDGAR current-filings feed filtered to the form: https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcurrent&type=SC+13E3&company=&dateb=&owner=include&count=40 . Fetched 2026-11-15: returned 1 entry (DoubleDown Interactive SC 13E3/A, accepted 2026-11-12 06:03) [V]. The feed only shows the last few days, so it must be polled daily; each hit then needs its text read for 'reverse stock split' and the threshold. EDGAR full-text search (efts.sec.gov) would do the text filter in one call but returned HTTP 403 to both my fetch attempts, so I could not confirm it from here; the repo's own EDGAR fetcher may reach it.
ideas.history_source: EDGAR form index for SC 13E3 (the repo already counts it: results/events/ss_catalogue/edgar_form_counts_by_year.csv), then filing text for ratio, threshold, cash price and effective date; CRSP daily for prices to 2025-12-31 and CRSP delisting records for the exit.
ideas.events_per_year: Upper bound: SC 13E3 by non-fund filers was 45 (2022), 48 (2023), 51 (2024), 36 (2025) [V: repo file edgar_form_counts_by_year.csv]; most of those are mergers. The split-cash-out subset is not counted. One web search surfaced four in 2025-26 (Tile Shop, Anebulo, Cyanotech, Ridgefield), of which two were exchange-listed with a threshold worth trading [S]. My guess is 3 to 8 usable a year [U]; the first test replaces the guess.
ideas.evidence: No academic study found. Evidence is filings only: Tile Shop terms [V/S as above]; Cyanotech 13E-3/A filed 2026-02-13, $0.47 per share for holders under 400 shares, total paid to cashed-out holders about $66,984 [V: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/768408/000094787126000143/ss5948989_sc13e3.htm]. Decay: unknown; the gap at Tile Shop was already under 3% the evening of the announcement.
ideas.main_risk: (1) Street-name treatment. Cyanotech's filing says nominees 'were instructed to effect' the split for beneficial holders but 'may have different procedures' [V]. If the broker's nominee position is not broken out per account, the holder is not cashed out and is left with a delisted share. Alpaca's handling is unknown and no paper account processes corporate actions (desk memory, 2026-10-28), so the shadow book would have to model the payment. (2) The board can abandon the plan or change the ratio so the position ends above the threshold. (3) Dollar profit per event is a few hundred dollars. (4) Thresholds below about 1,000 shares on a sub-$1 stock are not worth the ticket.
ideas.first_test: From the EDGAR index, list every non-fund SC 13E3 filed 2015-2025, keep those whose text has both a reverse and a forward split and a cash price, and tabulate: exchange-listed or not, threshold x price (maximum position), gap between the first post-filing close and the cash price, days to effective date, completed or abandoned. If fewer than 3 exchange-listed events a year have a maximum position above $5k and a gap above 2%, stop.

ideas.name: 2. Cash-shell biotech wind-downs, part A: the signed cash-plus-CVR buyout or board-approved dissolution
ideas.rule: Event: a biotech whose market value is below its net cash signs a definitive agreement to be bought for cash plus a non-tradeable contingent value right (the Concentra/Tang, XOMA Royalty pattern), or its board approves a plan of dissolution with a published per-share distribution range. Enter at the next close after the 8-K if price is at or below the cash component (or below the low end of the distribution range). Exit: cash at closing. For tender offers followed by a short-form merger no election is needed, since untendered shares are paid the same price in the merger; hold the CVR to expiry at zero carrying value. Long only; no hedge needed for the signed-deal leg.
ideas.why_it_pays: The buyer prices the bid at a discount to net cash and adds a CVR for cash above a floor and for asset sales. Generalist and index holders sell at or under the cash component because they cannot hold a non-tradeable CVR and do not want a micro-cap stub for six weeks. Loser: those sellers, who give the CVR away. Example terms: Elevation Oncology, $0.36 cash plus a CVR for all closing net cash above $26.4m and 80% of asset-sale proceeds (announced 2025-06-09) [V: BioPharma Dive]; CARGO Therapeutics, $4.379 plus a CVR for net cash above $217.5m, 'almost exactly' the prior close [S]; IGM Biosciences $1.247 plus CVR [S].
ideas.why_small: Deal values are tens of millions (Elevation about $21m [S]); the day-after-announcement float that trades below the cash component is thin; CVRs cannot be marked or lent, which rules out most funds with daily NAV.
ideas.live_source: EDGAR current-filings feed for third-party tender offers: https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcurrent&type=SC+TO-T&company=&dateb=&owner=include&count=100 . Fetched 2026-11-15: 3 filings from 2026-11-12/13 (EnerSys/Ultralife, Viatris/Pacira, DoubleU/DoubleDown) [V]. Serial bidder page: https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&company=concentra+biosciences&type=SC+TO-T returned Concentra Biosciences LLC, CIK 0001970065, with 3 original SC TO-T filings in 2025 (07-16, 07-21, 08-01) and none later on that page [V]. Net cash for the screen: SEC XBRL frames API, https://data.sec.gov/api/xbrl/frames/us-gaap/CashAndCashEquivalentsAtCarryingValue/USD/CY2026Q2I.json returned 4,337 companies for the 2026 Q2 balance date [V]. Dissolution plans arrive as 8-K and DEFM14A; I found no free feed that isolates them without the full-text search that was blocked to me.
ideas.history_source: SDC M&A on the desk's storage for cash deals with CVR consideration in SIC 2834/2836; EDGAR SC TO-T and DEFM14A text for CVR terms and dissolution ranges; XBRL frames for cash (2009 onward); CRSP daily and delisting payments to 2025-12-31.
ideas.events_per_year: Not counted by me. Press says Concentra alone had made 'at least its sixth deal this year' by the iTeos agreement in July 2025 [S: search summary]; the EDGAR page shows only 3 original SC TO-T under the parent CIK for 2025 [V], so the two disagree, probably because earlier offers were filed under merger-sub names. I found no Concentra deal dated 2026 in one search [V that the search returned none; not proof of none]. Working range 5 to 15 a year including dissolutions [U].
ideas.evidence: Practitioner only. Clark Street Value's mid-2025 review lists 8 open 'broken biotech' positions quoted below the author's liquidation estimates (for example MURA $2.50 against $3.25, HLVX $1.90 against about $2.50) and 7 closed ones, with no basket return given; the whole portfolio was -3.64% in H1 2025 [V: https://clarkstreetvalue.blogspot.com/2025/06/mid-year-2025-portfolio-review.html]. A third-party table puts that portfolio at -5.93% for 2025 and -6.4% for 2024 [S], which is evidence that the wider strategy has not been easy money recently. About one in six Nasdaq Biotechnology Index members traded below cash in July 2025 and an estimated $30bn sat idle in over 300 listed companies [V: Hedgeweek 2025-07-23, citing Bloomberg]. The XBI rallied strongly into 2026 [S], which likely shrank the pool.
ideas.main_risk: Net cash at closing lands below the floor so the cash price is cut or the CVR pays nothing; deal fails on a minimum-cash condition; a competing reverse merger replaces the cash bid; Irish or other non-US domiciles change the process [S]. The price at the first tradable close may already sit above the cash component, leaving nothing. CVR proceeds arrive a year or two later and paper accounts will not book them.
ideas.first_test: From SDC and EDGAR, list every 2019-2025 cash-plus-CVR acquisition and board-approved dissolution of a company in SIC 2834/2836 with market value below last-reported cash. For each: close on the day after the 8-K against the cash component, days to payment, cash actually paid, CVR payments made. Report the share of events where the next-day close was at or below the cash component, and the mean total received over that price. Fewer than 30 events, or a mean under 2% per event before CVR, and it is set aside.

ideas.name: 3. Cash-shell biotech wind-downs, part B: the pre-deal basket
ideas.rule: Event: a biotech files an 8-K announcing that it has stopped its lead programme, cut most of its staff and begun a review of 'strategic alternatives', and its market value at the next close is below a fixed fraction of net cash less one year of stated wind-down costs. Enter at the next close, equal weight. Exit: the close after a definitive deal, dissolution plan or reverse merger is announced, or after 250 sessions. Long basket against a short in XBI (shortable and easy to borrow at Alpaca on 2026-10-15 per the desk's catalogue).
ideas.why_it_pays: After the failure the holders who owned the science sell regardless of cash value, and activists (Tang Capital, BML, Soleus, BVF are named in practitioner notes [V: Clark Street Value]) then press for the cash to be returned. Loser: the sellers in the weeks after the trial failure. The return is the gap between price and what is eventually distributed or bid.
ideas.why_small: Market values of tens of millions, low float after insiders and activists, and outcome timing of two to twelve months with no mark. Third Harmonic announced liquidation about two months after starting its review [V: same post], others drift for a year.
ideas.live_source: No single free feed lists these. The usable route is the EDGAR current-filings feed for 8-K (same getcurrent endpoint, type=8-K, which I did not fetch for 8-K specifically) joined to SIC 2834/2836 and to the XBRL frames cash figure (fetched, 4,337 rows for CY2026Q2I [V]). The text filter ('strategic alternatives', 'workforce reduction') needs either the full-text search endpoint, which returned 403 to me, or downloading each 8-K. I am stating plainly that the live event list is not confirmed end to end.
ideas.history_source: EDGAR 8-K text (items 2.05 and 8.01) for SIC 2834/2836 filers, XBRL frames and company-facts for cash, marketable securities and debt, CRSP daily and delisting returns to 2025-12-31. IBES is not needed.
ideas.events_per_year: Not counted. The pool was large in 2025 (about one in six index members below cash [V: Hedgeweek]); the number that also announce a formal review in a given year is unknown [U]. The first test produces the count.
ideas.evidence: Practitioner write-ups only (Clark Street Value 2023-2025 posts [V for the June 2025 post]). The same author wrote in 2023 that there cannot be enough reverse-merger partners to go around [S], and in mid-2025 that he sees more to sell than to buy [V]. No published return series found. Treat any claim of a persistent premium as unproven; the 2021-2025 biotech bear market created the pool and the 2026 rally may have removed it.
ideas.main_risk: Management keeps spending (status-quo risk, named by the practitioner for HilleVax [V]); a dilutive reverse merger instead of a cash return; leases and severance larger than modelled; stale XBRL cash (a quarter old on the event date); a basket return that is just small-cap biotech beta, which is why the XBI hedge and a matched control of non-event negative-enterprise-value biotechs are part of the test.
ideas.first_test: Build the 2015-2025 event list from 8-K text, compute net cash from the last filing strictly before the event, and score the basket by shift(2) against XBI. Control group, declared now: biotechs below net cash on the same dates with no review announced. If the control earns as much, the event adds nothing.

ideas.name: 4. Converted thrifts: the first year after a standard mutual-to-stock conversion
ideas.rule: Event: a mutual savings institution completes a standard conversion and its shares begin trading (new 8-A12B registration by a savings-institution holding company, $10 offer price). Enter at the close of the second trading day, to stay out of the first-day jump. Exit at the close of the 250th session, before the period the literature finds weak. Long against a short in IWM or XLF (KRE was not shortable at Alpaca on 2026-10-15 per the desk's catalogue).
ideas.why_it_pays: Depositors buy at a price that includes the pre-existing capital for free, so the bank lists with excess capital at a discount to tangible book. Federal rule 12 CFR 239.63(c)(1) bars buybacks 'in the first year after the conversion' with narrow exceptions, 239.63(a) lets stock plans start within 12 months with a vote no earlier than six months, and 239.63(f)(1) bars anyone acquiring more than 10% 'for three years' [V: law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/12/239.63]. So there are dated steps: plan purchases from month six, buybacks from month twelve, sale of the bank from month thirty-six. Loser: depositors who sell their allocation in the first days.
ideas.why_small: Offerings are tens of millions and trade thinly; there are a handful a year; bank-holding rules make a large stake awkward.
ideas.live_source: EDGAR current-filings feed for new exchange registrations: https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcurrent&type=8-A12B&company=&dateb=&owner=include&count=100 . Fetched 2026-11-15: 30 entries from 2026-11-12 to 11-13, mostly ETFs and debt, none a thrift that day [V]. Filter by SIC 6035/6036; the SIC company list is at https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&SIC=6035&type=S-1 (fetched, 40 rows per page, no dates shown [V]). S&P Global's monthly 'State of the Pipeline' names each conversion but returned 403 to my fetch.
ideas.history_source: SDC new issues on the desk's storage (IPOs with SIC 6035/6036 at $10), cross-checked to EDGAR 424B3 and 8-A12B dates; CRSP daily to 2025-12-31.
ideas.events_per_year: Not counted from a primary. Search summaries of S&P's column name, for 2025: Magnolia Bancorp (began trading 2025-01-15, +11.2% first day), Avidia Bancorp and Security Midwest (both 2025-08-01, +46.4% and +14.0%), plus second-step deals at Lake Shore and Seneca; URSB Bancorp expected 2026-03-27; four to five in the pipeline in mid-2025 [S for all]. That is roughly 3 to 6 a year [S], too few for a stand-alone sleeve; it is a slow add-on.
ideas.evidence: Friesen and Swift, 'Overreaction in the Thrift IPO Aftermarket', Journal of Banking and Finance 33(7), 2009: after removing initial returns, cumulative excess returns are positive for the first 12 months, then a correction of about 18 months, with negative long-run returns concentrated in years two and three and strongest in small thrifts [V: abstract page, no magnitudes given; sample period not stated there]. First-day returns of 20.8% on 347 full conversions 1991-2004 in one study and about 7% in another [S]. The year-two-and-three weakness argues against the popular 'hold for the three-year takeover' version, which is why the rule exits at one year. Practitioners still hold these for the takeover date (NSTS Bancorp passed its three years in January 2025, quoted at $12.25 against about $15 tangible book [V: Clark Street Value]).
ideas.main_risk: The published pattern ends in the 2000s sample and may be gone; a handful of events a year gives no statistical power for years; the hedge is poor (regional-bank beta with no shortable regional-bank ETF); first-days prices are jumpy and paper fills at the quote will flatter the entry.
ideas.first_test: Count standard conversions and second steps per year 2005-2025 from SDC, then score the day-2-to-day-250 return against IWM by era. If 2013-2025 has fewer than 40 events or the post-2013 mean is not positive, record it and stop; also print months 13-36 to check the published reversal before anyone proposes the takeover-date version.

ideas.name: 5. Controller buyout proposals: buy the minority shares on the first public offer
ideas.rule: Event: a holder of more than 50% publicly proposes to buy the rest (a Schedule 13D amendment or company press release disclosing a non-binding offer). Enter at the next close. Exit at the close after a definitive agreement is announced, or after 120 sessions, or on withdrawal. Long, with a sector ETF short.
ideas.why_it_pays: The first offer goes to a special committee that usually negotiates; where a majority-of-the-minority vote is required, outside holders can also force more. Two cases in the paper below show 8% and 9% increases obtained through the minority vote condition after the committee had agreed a price [V]. Loser: the controller, who pays the increase.
ideas.why_small: Minority floats are small and illiquid, and the wait is months with no hedge for deal withdrawal.
ideas.live_source: EDGAR current-filings feed, type=SC 13E3 (fetched, see idea 1) gives the going-private filing, but that usually comes after the definitive agreement. The first-offer date needs Schedule 13D amendments (form type renamed 'SCHEDULE 13D' from 2024Q4 per the desk's catalogue) read for a proposal letter; I did not fetch that feed and know of no free list of first offers. Live source not confirmed.
ideas.history_source: SDC M&A on the desk's storage (acquirer stake above 50% before the deal, first-offer and final prices), EDGAR 13D/A and SC 13E3 for dates, CRSP daily.
ideas.events_per_year: Small. Restrepo and Subramanian's sample of all Delaware-target freezeouts from May 2013 to end-2024 is 34 before and 21 after the 2022-23 court decisions, 55 in about 11.6 years, under 5 a year, and only 'approximately half' are announced publicly at the first offer [V: paper, Table 1 and section text]. Non-Delaware targets add some. The 36 to 51 SC 13E3 filings a year in the repo's count include many other transaction types.
ideas.evidence: Restrepo and Subramanian, 'Declining MOM Conditions in Freezeout Transactions and the MOOM Alternative', UCLA working paper 2024 [V: https://escholarship.org/uc/item/0jw94422]: majority-of-the-minority conditions fell from about 80% of deals to about 45% after the 2022-23 decisions; the first-to-final price increase declined, not significantly; no average increase is stated in the parts I read. The fall in minority-vote conditions and Delaware's 2025 statute change (SB21, discussed in the paper) both weaken the minority's bargaining position, so the effect is more likely shrinking than growing. Earlier literature (Bates, Lemmon, Linck 2006; Subramanian 2007) is cited there but I did not open it [S].
ideas.main_risk: Too few events to test; the market prices the expected increase on day one (the paper notes prices 'reflect the offer price, any anticipated bump, and the likelihood of closing' [V]); withdrawals leave the share back at the pre-offer price; this may simply be the merger-arbitrage premium the desk already measured.
ideas.first_test: Count, from SDC, controller buyouts 2005-2025 with a public first offer and a CRSP price, and report first-offer-to-final price change and the return from the close after the first offer to the close after the agreement, by era. Below 60 events or a post-2013 mean under 3%, set aside.

ideas.name: 1. Crypto treasury companies below asset value: buy on the announcement of a coin-funded buyback, exit or wind-down, hedged with the coin ETF
ideas.rule: Universe: US-listed companies whose main asset is BTC or ETH and whose market value is below the value of the coins less debt. Event: an 8-K or press release that (a) starts or enlarges a buyback explicitly funded by selling coins, (b) announces a full exit from the treasury, a liquidation or a strategic review, or (c) discloses a 13D holder demanding one of those. Buy at the next close after the filing, short IBIT (or ETHA) for the coin exposure, hold 20 sessions or until the discount closes to a fixed level, whichever is first. This is the desk's closed-end-fund discount trade in a wrapper that has no 1940 Act rules.
ideas.why_it_pays: A buyback below asset value raises asset value per share mechanically, and a wind-down pays out close to asset value. The loser is the management that raised money at a premium in 2025 and the retail holder who sells at a deep discount; activists and boards are now being pushed to close the gap. Reported so far: ETHZilla sold about $40M of ETH on 2025-10-24 to buy back about 600,000 shares under a $250M authorisation and said it would keep selling until the discount normalised; the stock rose 14.5% that day (another report says 26% including after-hours) [S: The Block and Benzinga, 2025-10-27, via search, not opened]. FG Nexus sold ETH and bought stock at $3.45 against a reported $3.94 asset value [S]. SharpLink authorised up to $1.5B for use at or below asset value [S]. Sequans sold its last 314 BTC and exited [V: Cointelegraph 2026-09-24]. Those first-day jumps are NOT capturable at a next-close fill; the question is whether drift continues after it.
ideas.why_small: Most of these are micro and small caps with a short history, messy capital structures (convertibles, warrants, PIPE shares) and reputational baggage; a fund cannot size them and the law-firm literature treats them as an activism target, not an asset class. 16 of the 20 largest traded below asset value in September 2026 [V: Cointelegraph 2026-09-24, citing a DWF report]; at least 37 of the top 100 bitcoin treasuries were below it in early 2026 [V: Tally newsletter 2026-01-07].
ideas.live_source: Holdings: https://api.coingecko.com/api/v3/companies/public_treasury/bitcoin (free, no key) returned 181 companies, 83 with a US ticker, with coin counts and current value; the /ethereum endpoint returned 35 companies [V, both fetched today]. Of the 83 US bitcoin holders, 48 are in Cboe's optionable list [V: my join of the two fetched files]. Events: EDGAR 8-K and SC 13D current feeds (the desk already has EDGAR fetchers). I could NOT count events through EDGAR full-text search today: the endpoint returned 403 to a client without a declared contact [V], so the events-per-year figure is a gap. Shares outstanding and debt must come from each company's filings; CoinGecko does not carry them, so the discount itself needs a small build.
ideas.history_source: Thin, and that is the main weakness: the wave of these companies dates from 2025, so the sample is roughly October 2025 onward. Prices from CRSP daily to 2025-12-31 and Yahoo after; events hand-built from EDGAR 8-K text (search terms: 'net asset value' with 'repurchase', 'mNAV'). The closest long history is the desk's own closed-end-fund buyback, tender and liquidation work, which is a prior, not a test.
ideas.events_per_year: Not counted. Four named cases found in about thirteen months [S/V as above]. With 80-plus US names and most below asset value, a guess of one to three a month is [U] and must be replaced by an EDGAR count before any work.
ideas.evidence: No academic paper found. Practitioner and legal: Goodwin / Harvard Law corporate governance forum, 2026-09-14, says a 'substantial number' trade at or below asset value and that activists may push buybacks, liquidation or mergers [V]; Bitwise's Hougan argues a same-day liquidation would price at 1.0x and a one-year wind-down justifies a discount [S]. Nothing here has had time to decay; equally nothing is proven.
ideas.main_risk: The discount can be deserved: ongoing share issuance, management fees and costs, debt ahead of the equity, coins that are staked or pledged. A coin-funded buyback can be the start of a forced unwind ('death spiral' was the press reaction to ETHZilla [S]). The first-day jump is gone before a next-close fill. Asset value needs share counts that go stale between filings, which is the stale-price trap in a new form. Small sample: tens of events at most. The IBIT hedge needs IBIT to be shortable at Alpaca on the day; check, do not assume.
ideas.first_test: Zero-return census first: from EDGAR, list every 8-K since 2025-06 by the 83 + 35 companies that mentions a repurchase or sale of digital assets; count events and distinct issuers. If under 20 events, stop and keep it as a watch list. If 20 or more, measure the 20-session return from the next close after filing, less IBIT/ETHA beta, and compare with the same companies on random non-event dates (the control that has killed most ideas here).

ideas.name: 2. Single-stock leveraged ETFs: the forced trade at the close in the underlying share
ideas.rule: Each day at about 15:45 ET, for every stock that has 2x or inverse single-stock ETFs, compute forced flow = sum over its funds of AUM x L x (L-1) x the stock's return so far today (2 x AUM x r for a 2x fund, 6 x AUM x r for a -2x fund). When forced flow exceeds a pre-set share of the stock's median closing-auction volume and the stock is down on the day, buy at the close and sell at the next open (or next close); the mirror on up days is a short and only for easy-to-borrow names. Extends catalogue row J9, which was framed on SPY, QQQ and IWM and is still waiting for a ruling.
ideas.why_it_pays: A daily-reset leveraged fund must trade in the direction of the day's move, near the close, whatever the price. The loser is the fund's holders, who pay the impact. Barbon, Beckmeyer, Buraschi and Moerke (SSRN 3925725, 2021-22) find end-of-day momentum from these flows that is gone within the next day, and that the leveraged-ETF part was shrinking in their sample, which predates single-stock funds [S: abstract via search]. The single-stock case is different in size: a May 2026 practitioner note puts flagship fund assets at 19 to 23% of the underlying's daily dollar volume (TSLL, NVDL, MSTU) against a closing auction of about 10% of daily volume [V: quidprokuo.github.io/drift/letf-rebalancing-costs, 2026-05-30; the note's impact figures are a toy model, not measurements].
ideas.why_small: The effect is largest where the fund is big relative to a small or mid-sized underlying (quantum, crypto-treasury and small AI names), which are exactly the names a large liquidity provider cannot hold overnight in size. More than 450 leveraged and inverse single-security ETFs have launched since 2022 [S: Bloomberg Opinion via Wealth Management, July 2026, not opened]. Many showed up in the desk's own reverse-split feed (MSTU, QBTX, RGTZ, AXTU and others) [V: results/ideas/reverse_splits/borrow_now.json].
ideas.live_source: Daily fund assets and shares outstanding on issuer pages, e.g. https://www.rexshares.com/mstu/ returned net assets $369,469,518, shares outstanding 18,326,861, NAV $20.17 as of 2026-11-12 [V]. No CSV there; each issuer (REX, Defiance, Direxion, GraniteShares, Tradr, Leverage Shares) needs its own scraper, or use shares outstanding x price from a market-data feed. The intraday return comes from Alpaca's own data feed at run time. The list of funds: Cboe symbol directory and issuer product lists.
ideas.history_source: CRSP daily on the desk's storage: ETF shares outstanding x price gives fund assets by day to 2025-12-31, and the underlying's open, close and volume are there too. Closing-auction volume is not in CRSP; use total volume as the denominator and say so. Close-to-next-open needs CRSP's open price field.
ideas.events_per_year: Not counted. Depends on the threshold; the population is several hundred funds on perhaps 100 to 150 underlyings [U], so a 'large flow and stock down 5%+' day should occur hundreds of times a year across names. Count it from CRSP before anything else.
ideas.evidence: Index-level effect documented and decaying (Barbon et al. 2021-22) [S]. Bessembinder, 'Leveraged Single-Stock ETFs' (August 2025) is about holder returns, not close impact [S]. I found no paper measuring the close effect in single-stock underlyings; that is the gap this idea sits in.
ideas.main_risk: The desk's C5 (next-open fill) died as ordinary session drift and X2/X3 as calendar flows, so the control must be declared first: the same stock on equally large down days before its leveraged fund existed, and matched stocks with no such fund. Swap dealers may hedge through the afternoon, not at the close, so the pressure may already be in the 15:45 price. A down-5% day in a small stock is also just short-term reversal, which the desk already measured as weak on the long side since 2013. Overnight gap risk in volatile names. The decision time (15:45) is after the desk's usual evening decision; it fits the paper 'late market' path but not a 15:50 MOC cut-off without care.
ideas.first_test: The J9 gate, re-aimed: for each underlying-day in CRSP 2023-2025, forced flow as a share of that day's volume. If it is under 1% of volume on 95% of large-move days, kill at zero trials. If not, one pre-set test: close-to-next-open return on days with the stock down 5% or more, split by forced-flow tercile, against the two controls above.

ideas.name: 3. Weekend crypto moves and the Monday session in crypto-linked stocks
ideas.rule: Each Monday before the open, compute the BTC (and ETH) return from Friday 16:00 ET to Monday 09:25 ET from a public exchange feed. On weekends with a move beyond a pre-set size, trade the crypto-linked stocks (miners, treasury companies, exchanges) against IBIT from Monday's open to Monday's close: the direction is set by the first test, not assumed. Instruments are stocks and IBIT, so no crypto fees.
ideas.why_it_pays: Crypto trades through the weekend and its listed proxies do not, so every Monday open has to absorb two days of news at once. The spot ETF reprices mechanically; small miners and treasury companies are repriced by retail orders queued over the weekend, which is where over- or under-shooting would sit. The loser is whoever sends market-on-open orders in thin names. Published: Mourey, Shahrour and Soiman, 'A crypto-stock weekend effect', Finance Research Letters 86 (2025): negative weekend crypto returns predict Monday equity declines, positive ones do not, across Nasdaq, Russell 2000, sectors and the S&P crypto index, stronger after May 2022 [V: abstract on ideas.repec.org; the full text was blocked, so effect sizes and whether 'Monday return' includes the opening gap are NOT known]. One case: on 2026-02-02 MSTR was down 6.7% pre-market after a weekend fall although bitcoin had by then recovered about 1% [S: CoinDesk via search].
ideas.why_small: Fifty-odd Mondays a year, of which perhaps ten to fifteen have a large weekend move, in a basket where the interesting names are small. Too few bets and too little size for a fund; fine for one account.
ideas.live_source: Weekend coin prices: any public exchange candle API (Coinbase or Kraken public market data; not fetched today, they are standard and keyless [U]). Basket membership: https://api.coingecko.com/api/v3/companies/public_treasury/bitcoin, 83 US tickers [V]. Stock opens and closes: the desk's Alpaca data at run time.
ideas.history_source: CRSP daily open and close for the stocks to 2025-12-31, Yahoo for 2026; public hourly BTC and ETH history from exchange APIs; IBIT exists only from January 2024, so before that the hedge is BTC itself close-to-close and the test is on the stocks alone.
ideas.events_per_year: About 52 Mondays; large-move weekends not counted. Count them from the BTC series for whatever threshold is fixed in advance (for example beyond one daily standard deviation).
ideas.evidence: The paper above (2025). A Crypto.com research note (April 2026) on tokenised-stock perpetuals reports the Sunday 22:00 UTC price predicting the Monday gap direction 53 to 79% of the time for NVDA, TSLA and Nasdaq on 19 to 23 weekends, and that trading it lost money on the short side [V: crypto.com/uk/research/rwa-perps-find-predictive-edge-apr-2026]. That is evidence the gap itself is priced before the open; nothing found on what happens after the open in crypto stocks.
ideas.main_risk: The most likely outcome is that the published effect is the opening gap, which cannot be bought. Overnight and pre-market trading now exists in these names, so the open may already be efficient. Open prints in small names are noisy and the open-auction fill is the thing C5 failed on. Borrow on small miners for the short half. Speculative; labelled as such.
ideas.first_test: One afternoon on data in hand: for 2020-2025, regress Monday open-to-close return of an equal-weight miner and treasury basket (less BTC's return over the same hours) on the weekend BTC return, separately for negative and positive weekends, and again for the Friday-close-to-Monday-open gap. If all the predictability is in the gap and none after the open, close it.

ideas.name: 4. Reverse splits through puts: the borrow the desk could not find, priced from the option chain
ideas.rule: For each reverse split in a stock that has listed options, on the ex-date read the chain and compute the borrow cost implied by put-call parity (the gap between the synthetic short and the stock). Where the implied cost over the next 20 to 30 sessions is well under the 9% fall the desk measured, buy a put spread (at-the-money long, about 20% out short) expiring after day 21; close at day 21. No stock borrow needed.
ideas.why_it_pays: The desk's own card found about 9% in 20 sessions against IWM after a reverse split and set it aside only because Alpaca would not lend the shares (results/ideas/2026-11-15_reverse_splits.md) [V]. A put is the listed way to be short without a locate. The loser is the same as in the stock version: holders who do not sell into continued dilution. The open question is only whether the option market has already charged for it.
ideas.why_small: Open interest in these chains is tiny, the series become non-standard after the split, and spreads are wide: a few contracts per name at most.
ideas.live_source: Which names have options: Cboe symbol directory CSV, 5,410 rows [V]. The chain with bid, ask and IV: https://cdn.cboe.com/api/global/delayed_quotes/options/{SYM}.json [V: fetched for MARA]. Reverse-split events: the Alpaca corporate-actions feed the desk already reads. Count made today by joining the desk's snapshot (results/ideas/reverse_splits/borrow_now.json, read 2026-11-15) to the Cboe list: of 483 feed rows the card marked eligible in the last year, 158 have options today; of the 217 with $5M a day, 103; of the 118 within 90 days, 29; but of the 32 the book would hold now (ex-date within 30 days) only 3 (COSM, KNDI, LU) [V]. Many of the optionable rows are leveraged single-stock ETFs, not companies.
ideas.history_source: None that is free. The desk's option store covers six ETFs only [V: docs/DATA.md]. This can only be tested forward by saving chains daily, or with a purchased history. Say this plainly in any card.
ideas.events_per_year: About 3 of 32 currently held names, so roughly 10% of events; on the card's own count of eligible events that is on the order of a few dozen optionable events a year, fewer once leveraged ETFs are removed [V for the 3 of 32; the yearly figure is an extrapolation, U].
ideas.evidence: The desk's own price result [V]. General finding that option prices embed the cost of borrowing hard-to-borrow shares is standard put-call parity; no reverse-split-specific options study found.
ideas.main_risk: Most likely the puts already cost the drift: when shares cannot be borrowed, the synthetic short trades below the stock by the borrow fee, and implied volatility on these names is very high. Adjusted series after the split may not be tradable to open at Alpaca (its options page does not say [V]); options are usually listed on the larger names, where the card did not test whether the fall is the same. Wide spreads can eat a 9% edge twice over.
ideas.first_test: No history needed: for the next 30 days, each evening pull the Cboe chain for every reverse-split name inside its 21-session window that has options, and record the parity-implied borrow, the mid and the bid-ask of the at-the-money put. If the implied cost to day 21 plus half the spread is above about 9% on most names, close the idea for good and record that the option market prices it.

ideas.name: 5. Sprott Physical Uranium Trust: its premium or discount as a switch for uranium equities (speculative, live source not fetched)
ideas.rule: The trust can sell new units, and so buy physical uranium, only when its units trade above the prior day's asset value. Signal: the day the trust moves from a discount to a premium (or announces a financing), go long a US-listed uranium ETF (URNM or URA) for a fixed window; stand aside while it trades at a discount. A second, simpler form: none of this, just a regime flag for any uranium position.
ideas.why_it_pays: Spot uranium is a thin market, and the trust is a price-insensitive buyer that is switched on and off by its own premium. The loser is the utility or trader who has to buy spot after the trust has. Reported: the spot price rose almost 9% on 2025-06-16 after the trust announced a $100M raise [S: S&P Global headline via search, not opened]; the issuance rule is in the prospectus supplement and S&P's description [S].
ideas.why_small: A handful of switches a year in one commodity; the trust itself trades in Toronto and over the counter, so most US quant screens do not carry it at all.
ideas.live_source: NOT fetched. Sprott's fund page (sprott.com/uranium) returned HTTP 500 on two attempts today. A search snippet of that page reports the trust at a discount of about 16% on 2026-11-06, with 239 days at a discount in 2025 and no day at a premium in Q3 2026 [S, unverified]. If that is right the switch is currently off and has been for a long time.
ideas.history_source: Trust price and asset value history from Sprott's site if it offers a download (not confirmed); URNM, URA and miner prices from CRSP and Yahoo; financing announcements from SEDAR+ and press releases. The trust only dates from July 2021.
ideas.events_per_year: Unknown; low single digits by the look of it, and possibly zero in the last year. This is a rare-event idea and should be judged as one.
ideas.evidence: Press and analyst commentary only ('the Sprott effect'); no controlled study found. Five years of history.
ideas.main_risk: Too few events to prove anything; the equities may move before the premium flips, since the premium is itself driven by the same sentiment; the trust is not tradable on a US exchange so only the indirect leg is available; the live figures above are unverified.
ideas.first_test: Get the daily premium/discount series from Sprott (or build it from price and published asset value), count discount-to-premium crossings and financings since 2021, and stop if there are fewer than 15.

ideas.name: 1. Unit-trust deposit and termination flows in closed-end funds (EDGAR form 487)
ideas.rule: Parse every form 487 (unit investment trust prospectus) whose portfolio is closed-end funds. Each gives the tickers, weights, deposit date and Mandatory Termination Date. (a) Termination leg, long only: for each CEF held by a terminating series, buy at the close of the Mandatory Termination Date (the forced sale window is the nine business days before it) and hold 10 sessions, hedged with PCEF or an equal-weight basket of CEFs not in the series. Weight by the flow as a share of the CEF's ADV; give double weight to names that are NOT in the sponsor's successor series (no rollover buying offsets them). (b) Deposit leg: on a new 487, diff the portfolio against the previous series of the same strategy; buy names newly added at the next close and hold through the offering period (about 20 to 30 sessions), same hedge.
ideas.why_it_pays: A UIT is a fixed portfolio with a termination date written in the prospectus. The trustee must sell everything in a short, stated window regardless of price, and the sponsor must buy the stated basket as units sell. The filing I read says the trustee 'may begin to sell Securities ... as early as nine business days prior to, but will sell Securities no later than, the Mandatory Termination Date' and that 'because the Trustee must sell the Securities within a relatively short period of time' the sale may reduce proceeds [V: FT 13398, 487 filed 2026-11-13]. The loser is the unit-holder, who pays the price concession on a forced sale in funds whose ADV is about $0.4m to $1.2m (repo census medians [S: CEF_CORP_ACTION_CENSUS_2026-10-15.md]). It is a dated, mechanical flow that the desk's z-score cannot see, in exactly the funds the desk already trades (the series I read holds HYT, DSL, PHK, HIX, HIO, ACP, BGH and 12 others at 2 to 7% each [V]).
ideas.why_small: The per-fund flow is tens of thousands of dollars a day. No institutional desk parses unit-trust prospectuses for $50k of daily price pressure; the series themselves are retail broker products. I found no paper and no practitioner write-up on it (two searches, negative [S]).
ideas.live_source: EDGAR full-text search, form 487: https://efts.sec.gov/LATEST/search-index?q=%22closed-end%22&forms=487&dateRange=custom&startdt=2026-10-01&enddt=2026-11-15 returned 154 document hits for six weeks, from First Trust (FT series), Guggenheim Defined Portfolios, Invesco Unit Trusts, SmartTrust and Advisors Disciplined Trust [V]. The prospectus itself: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2154589/000144554626008650/s487.htm (High-Yield Income Closed-End Portfolio, Series 127: 19 CEFs with tickers, share counts and weights; deposit 2026-11-13; Mandatory Termination Date 2028-11-13) [V]. Series size: the series' own form 24F-2NT, e.g. FT 10882 (the same strategy, deposited 2023-08-02) reports $9,627,365.98 of units sold by its 2023-09-19 fiscal year-end [V: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1976499/000144554623006987/primary_doc.xml]. Terminations are known two years ahead, so the live calendar is built from old filings.
ideas.history_source: EDGAR 487 filings back to 2001 (full-text search) for portfolios and dates; 24F-2NT for units sold per series; CRSP daily on the desk's storage for CEF prices and volume (1,123 CEFs, dead ones included, to 2025-12-31 per the cef_exdate_drift card [S]). Everything is point-in-time: the 487 is filed on the deposit date.
ideas.events_per_year: 487 documents mentioning 'closed-end funds': 447 (2019), 305 (2022), 377 (2024), 365 (2025) [V, EDGAR full-text hit counts; these count documents, and include diversified trusts that hold only a few CEFs]. 2023: 335 hits from at least 291 distinct series CIKs [V]. Units sold in the first fiscal year, sample of 58 of those 2023 series: median $28.7m, range $2.8m to $75.5m [V, 24F-2NT]. Caveat: that sample is every series whose prospectus mentions closed-end funds, not CEF-only portfolios; the one pure CEF series I checked sold $9.6m. Each series is one deposit event and one termination event, each touching 15 to 60 funds.
ideas.evidence: None published that I could find [S, negative search]. Sizing from fetched numbers: a $9.6m series at 2 to 7% per fund is $190k to $670k per CEF, sold within nine business days, i.e. roughly $20k to $75k a day against CEF ADV of $0.4m to $1.2m (arithmetic on [V] and [S] inputs): 2 to 15% of volume for the smaller funds, more when several sponsors' series terminate together. The mechanism is the same forced-flow family as the desk's month-end Treasury book; nothing here says it has been arbitraged or decayed because nothing says it has been studied.
ideas.main_risk: (1) Rollover: holders who roll into the successor series cause the sponsor to buy much the same basket in the same days, so net flow may be near zero for names kept; the effect should live in dropped and added names only, which cuts the event count. (2) Size at termination is unknown: 24F-2NT gives units sold, not units left after two years of redemptions. (3) The flow may simply be too small against ADV; (4) early termination and in-kind distributions; (5) the deposit leg is slow (weeks), so it is easily confused with discount reversion: the control group is same-category CEFs not in the series.
ideas.first_test: No returns yet. Build the flow table: for all CEF-portfolio 487s 2010 to 2022, compute per fund per day the scheduled termination sale (units sold x weight / 9 days) as a share of CRSP dollar volume, separately for names kept and names dropped by the successor series. Kill if the 90th percentile is under 5% of ADV or there are fewer than 100 dropped-name events a year. If it survives, one event study: market-adjusted return of terminating-series names over days -9..0 and 0..+10 around the Mandatory Termination Date, against same-category CEFs not held.

ideas.name: 2. Royalty-trust monthly distributions: predictable from commodity prices already published
ideas.rule: Each month, for every exchange-listed oil and gas royalty trust that pays monthly, predict the change in the coming distribution from the change in the WTI and Henry Hub monthly average for the production month the payment will cover (about two months earlier, already public). If the predicted change is in the top third (large rise), buy the units 5 sessions before the expected announcement date and sell 3 sessions after the 8-K; hedge with XOP or a basket of the other trusts. Skip (do not short) the predicted cuts unless borrow exists.
ideas.why_it_pays: The trust is a pass-through: the distribution is last period's volumes times prices from about two months back, less costs. One write-up states distributions 'reflect commodity prices on a roughly two-month lag' and that a Sabine payment covered oil from April and gas from March [S: 247wallst 2026-05-04 and panabee, via search summary]. Units are held by retail income buyers who price on the trailing yield and react to the announced figure: Sabine fell on 2024-12-05 after announcing a distribution down almost 45% on the month [S: Yahoo Finance headline via search]. If the announced change is largely knowable weeks earlier, the reaction is to stale news. The loser is the yield buyer who waits for the press release.
ideas.why_small: About a dozen trusts, market caps mostly under $1bn, no analyst coverage, no index weight. A fund cannot put money to work and the modelling is per-trust clerical work (hedges, cost carry-forwards, net-profits-interest deficits).
ideas.live_source: EDGAR per-trust filing feed: https://data.sec.gov/submissions/CIK0000319654.json (Permian Basin Royalty Trust, PBT, NYSE) returned 318 8-Ks, 12 to 17 a year every year since 2004, the monthly ones under item 2.02 with acceptance timestamps (e.g. 2026-10-20T15:06:50Z, 2026-09-18, 2026-08-21) [V]. Commodity inputs: FRED CSV https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=DHHNGSP returned daily Henry Hub to 2026-11-11 (3.00) [V]; DCOILWTICO is the matching WTI series [U, not fetched today].
ideas.history_source: CRSP distributions (declaration date and amount) and CRSP daily for the trust units: the desk's units panel already carries royalty trusts (results/ideas/2026-11-11_exdate_other_wrappers.md, 242 units with eligible ex-dates [S]). EDGAR 8-K acceptance times for announcement timing back to 2004; FRED for prices. Note the desk's units ex-date book already holds these names around the ex-date, so the announcement window must be tested net of that.
ideas.events_per_year: 8-Ks in 2025 matching "Royalty Trust" + "distribution" + "record": 157 document hits; by filer PBT 23, PermRock (PRT) 19, Sabine (SBR) 18, Cross Timbers (CRT) 17, Permianville (PVL) 12, Mesa (MTR) 12, Pacific Coast Oil Trust 12 (not exchange-listed [U]), North European (NRT) 4, Marine Petroleum (MARPS) 4, BP Prudhoe 3 [V, EDGAR full-text search; counts include exhibits]. So about 70 to 90 monthly announcements a year on six listed monthly payers, plus quarterly payers; San Juan Basin, MV Oil and VOC did not match my phrase and are not counted.
ideas.evidence: Anecdote only; I found no academic study of royalty-trust distribution predictability (one search, negative [S]). This is a labelled speculation with a clear mechanism. Related, proven on the desk's own data: the units ex-date pattern (shadow books units_exdate_*), which shows the same retail clientele misprices dated cash events in these units.
ideas.main_risk: (1) The market may already price the lag: these trusts trade with oil and gas daily, so the 'surprise' may be nil. (2) Distribution noise unrelated to prices (cost deficits, operator true-ups, skipped payments: San Juan fell more than 17% on 2021-08-20 on a skipped payment [S: Motley Fool via search]) dominates in several trusts. (3) Around 80 events a year in six correlated names is one commodity bet unless hedged. (4) Spreads and thin volume in PRT, MTR, PVL. (5) Overlap with the existing units ex-date book.
ideas.first_test: From CRSP distributions, regress the month-on-month change in each trust's distribution on the change in the lagged WTI and Henry Hub monthly averages, fitted on data before each date. If the out-of-sample R-squared is below about 0.3 the idea is dead (nothing to predict). If it holds, one event study: return from 5 sessions before to 3 after the declaration date, sorted on the predicted change, hedged with XOP, 2005 to 2022, by era.

ideas.name: 3. Saba's footprint: the activist's own ETF holdings and 13D/13G filings as a buy list
ideas.rule: Each day read the published holdings of the Saba Closed-End Funds ETF (CEFS) and each evening the day's SCHEDULE 13D/13G filings by Saba, Karpus, Bulldog and City of London. Buy a CEF at the next close when (a) it appears in CEFS for the first time or its share count rises by more than a set fraction, or (b) a first 13D or a 13G crossing 5% is filed; hold 60 sessions or until a tender or settlement is announced; hedge with the fund's category ETF (HYG, MUB, SPY as the repo's census does).
ideas.why_it_pays: An activist that keeps buying is a persistent bidder, and a campaign ends in a tender, liquidation or open-ending near NAV. Bradley, Brav, Goldstein and Jiang (JFE 2010, sample 1988 to 2003) find discounts narrow around and in anticipation of open-ending attempts [S: search summary of the paper; not opened]. The loser is the long-term retail holder who sells to the activist at a wide discount. The desk's z-score ranks a fund against its own history and cannot see who is accumulating.
ideas.why_small: The targets are $100m to $1bn funds trading under $1m a day; Saba itself is the only large player and it publishes its ETF book. The desk already counted the raw material: 230 initial activist 13Ds in 2010 to 2022, 17.7 a year, and 80 proxy contests, scored 'none' only because no exit price is stated, never tested as an event return [S: CEF_CORP_ACTION_CENSUS_2026-10-15.md].
ideas.live_source: https://www.sabaetf.com/cefs: the page returned a holdings table headed 'Holdings as of 11/12/2026' with columns company name, ticker, FIGI, shares, market value and % of net assets, and a 'Download As CSV' control; the rows and the CSV URL are rendered by script and did not come through my fetch, so the row-level file is NOT confirmed fetched [V for the page and date, U for the file]. Filings: EDGAR daily index and full-text search for SCHEDULE 13D/13G (the repo notes the form was renamed from 'SC 13D' in 2024Q4 [S]).
ideas.history_source: EDGAR SC 13D/13G and amendments since 2008 (the desk's census already holds the episode table); CEFS monthly holdings from its N-PORT filings on EDGAR (quarter-ends public; monthly public from 2027-11-17 per the repo's compliance calendar [S]); CRSP daily CEF prices. Daily CEFS holdings history is not archived anywhere free that I found, so branch (a) can only be tested forward or on monthly N-PORT snapshots.
ideas.events_per_year: 17.7 initial activist 13Ds a year and 6.2 proxy contests a year in CEFs, 2010 to 2022 [S: repo census, counted from EDGAR]. CEFS position changes: not counted (rows not fetched).
ideas.evidence: Bradley et al. 2010 (1988 to 2003) [S]. Regime change the desk already tracks: control-share rulings (2nd Circuit, Saba v. Nuveen, 2023-11-30) and the June 2026 Supreme Court section 47(b) ruling noted in the task brief changed the activist toolkit, so pre-2023 returns may not carry over; test by era. The NAV-tender trade that often follows was tested by the desk and was significant gross but not net of 15bp [S: NAV_TENDER_RESULT_2026-10-20.md].
ideas.main_risk: The discount may close on the filing day, leaving nothing after a next-close entry (the paper says the market anticipates attacks). Heavy overlap with the desk's own discount-reversion book: activists buy wide discounts, which the z-score already buys, so the control is same-discount funds with no filing. Many targets sit in the desk's sealed holdout names. Campaigns cluster in a few sponsors (few independent groups).
ideas.first_test: Using the existing census episodes only: market- and category-adjusted return from the close after the first 13D to +60 sessions, 2010 to 2022, against matched funds with the same discount z-score and no filing. Kill if the matched control earns the same.

ideas.name: 4. December tax-loss selling in $25-par preferreds and baby bonds, bought for the January rebound
ideas.rule: On the tenth trading day of December rank all exchange-listed $25-par preferreds and baby bonds by year-to-date price return; buy the worst fifth that still pay their dividend (no issuer in default or arrears), equal weight, capped by volume; sell on the tenth trading day of January; hedge with a short in PFF or PGX (both easy to borrow per the repo).
ideas.why_it_pays: Individual preferreds are held by taxable retail accounts; the tax value of a realised loss exceeds the price concession, so losers are sold into year-end and recover when the selling stops. Vetter and Wingender (Quarterly Journal of Business and Economics, 1996) report a significant positive January return in a preferred index and in individual issues [S: abstract via search; not opened]. A practitioner weekly titled 'Year-End Tax Losers Rally Hard' described the same pattern in preferreds [S: Seeking Alpha article 4570064, title only]. The loser is the tax seller, knowingly.
ideas.why_small: The typical issue trades a few hundred thousand dollars a day; only about a tenth are shortable (45 of 422 preferreds, 5 of 168 baby bonds at Alpaca on the repo's 2026-10-19 census [S]), so no long-short fund can run it, and it is one trade a year.
ideas.live_source: Universe: the desk's own Alpaca census, results/events/ss_catalogue_credit/alpaca_listed_fixed_income_2026-10-15.csv (547 rows of listed preferreds and baby bonds with tradable and shortable flags) [V, file read]. Prices: Alpaca daily bars at run time (not called by me); free cross-check, Yahoo chart endpoint https://query1.finance.yahoo.com/v8/finance/chart/BAC-PB?range=max returned history from 2018-05-07 to 2026-11-13, and NLY-PF from 2017-07-24 [V]. The first live window opens in about four weeks.
ideas.history_source: Weak, and this is the main gap. CRSP's stock file does not carry most preferreds [U: my recollection; check the R2 mirror's share types]. Yahoo returned nothing for a redeemed issue (CIO-PA: no data [V]), so a free backtest is survivor-only: called and defaulted issues are missing. Alpaca's bars for inactive symbols may fill this [U, not tested: no Alpaca calls allowed here].
ideas.events_per_year: One season a year; cross-section about 420 preferreds and 170 baby bonds today [S: repo census 2026-10-19], so roughly 100 names in the bottom fifth. By the desk's own counting rule this is one independent event a year.
ideas.evidence: Vetter and Wingender 1996 [S]; practitioner commentary [S]. The desk closed the muni-CEF version as a sleeve (CORE-b: kept as a stratum only [S: RESEARCH_STATE.md]) and queued the all-CEF version (hunt card 10); preferreds have not been looked at. Decay unknown.
ideas.main_risk: The worst performers in a year are the issuers heading for suspension or default: the rebound average can hide a few total losses, and a survivor-only price history hides exactly those. One event a year means decades to prove. Rate moves in January swamp the effect unless the PFF hedge is well matched. Wide spreads on the cheapest names.
ideas.first_test: Before any return: establish whether a delisting-inclusive price history for preferreds exists on the desk's storage or at Alpaca. If yes, run the fixed rule on every December from the first available year, PFF-hedged, reporting each year separately and the count of names that defaulted or suspended in the window. If no such history exists, run it forward on paper this December as a labelled forward test, small.

ideas.name: 5. The target's listed preferred in a cash takeover
ideas.rule: When a merger agreement is filed for an issuer with an exchange-listed preferred, read the agreement for the preferred's treatment. If it is to be redeemed or converted to cash at $25 plus accrued, and the preferred closes below that value less a set margin on the day after the 8-K, buy and hold to closing. If it is to remain outstanding under a private or weaker owner, do not hold (and exit any existing position).
ideas.why_it_pays: The common is watched by merger-arbitrage funds within minutes; the preferred's treatment sits in the merger agreement and its holders are retail income accounts. Two outcomes diverge sharply: cash at liquidation preference, or an orphaned, possibly delisted security. Preferred terms differ by issue: one prospectus I was shown gives the issuer only an option to redeem at $25 on a change of control and says a merger is not a liquidation (Global Medical REIT Series B, 424B5 2025 [S: search summary]). The loser is the holder who sells below the cash value, or who holds through an orphaning.
ideas.why_small: A typical listed preferred is $50m to $200m outstanding and trades thinly; the position a fund could take is not worth a lawyer's hour on the certificate of designation.
ideas.live_source: EDGAR full-text search on merger proxies and 8-Ks, e.g. https://efts.sec.gov/LATEST/search-index?q=%22Cumulative%20Redeemable%20Preferred%20Stock%22%20%22Agreement%20and%20Plan%20of%20Merger%22%20%22New%20York%20Stock%20Exchange%22&forms=DEFM14A returned filers by year [V]; in live use the trigger is the 8-K item 1.01 with the merger agreement, joined to the repo's listed-preferred census by CIK (97.8% of issues mapped to a CIK [S: SS_DESK_EXPANSION_2026-10-19.md]).
ideas.history_source: SDC M&A on the desk's storage joined to EDGAR merger agreements for the treatment; prices are the problem, as in idea 4: preferreds of acquired issuers are delisted and absent from Yahoo (CIO-PA returned no data [V]); needs Alpaca inactive-symbol bars or another delisting-inclusive source [U].
ideas.events_per_year: Merger proxies (DEFM14A) mentioning a cumulative redeemable preferred and the NYSE: 3 (2018), 1 (2019), 4 (2020), 5 (2021), 4 (2022), 9 (2023), 0 (2024), 4 (2025) distinct filers [V, EDGAR full-text search; a narrow phrase that misses bank non-cumulative preferreds and stock deals on S-4, and includes some filers whose preferred is not the target's]. Call it 3 to 10 a year: small by any standard.
ideas.evidence: No study found. The 2022 Cedar Realty deal (in the count above) is the known case of preferreds left outstanding after a sale [U: recalled, not fetched]. Nothing on decay.
ideas.main_risk: Too few events to ever reach significance; the price may jump to the cash value on the announcement day, leaving only a bill-like carry; reading the treatment is legal text that a script will misread; no free delisting-inclusive price history; closing risk is the same as the common's.
ideas.first_test: Zero-return census: for the 30 filers found above, record from the merger agreement the preferred's treatment and, where a price exists, the gap between the first close after the 8-K and the cash value. If the median gap is under 1% or fewer than half the cases are cash-redeemed, drop it and keep only the orphaning rule as a risk flag for any preferred the desk holds.

verdicts.name: 1. Thrift mutual-to-stock conversions: hold the first year, leave before the second
verdicts.already_on_desk: Not tested. No card in results/ideas/, nothing in docs/RESEARCH_STATE.md or results/events/ (the only 'thrift' hits are an R2 table inventory and a merger deal list). Nearest neighbour is results/ideas/2026-11-15_ipo_lockups.md, a different mechanism.
verdicts.source_check: EDGAR full-text search re-fetched 2026-11-15, HTTP 200 [V]. With forms 424B3 and S-1 for 2026-01-01 to 2026-11-15 I get 81 documents from 8 issuers, not the scout's 6: PSB Financial, Rhinebeck (RBKB), CSB Financial, Hometown Financial Group (HFG), MFB Bancorp (MFDB), Columbia Financial, URSB Bancorp, Narragansett Bancorp; newest filing 2026-11-13 [V]. The scout's count used 424B3 only; I am reporting the difference, not reconciling it. Only 3 of the 8 show a ticker in EDGAR [V]. The prospectus arrives months ahead, so notice is ample, but the first trading day is NOT in this feed; it needs the issuer's 8-K or a new Alpaca symbol, and nobody has checked that. Alpaca tradability checked in principle only (the probe reads config/.env, which I may not): exchange-listed names long-only are fine, OTC ones are not.
verdicts.strongest_objection: The rule mixes two different events. A second-step (Rhinebeck, Columbia) is already listed, so 'shares start trading' and 'starts below tangible book' do not apply the same way; they must be split before any return is read. The supporting paper's own headline is negative long-run risk-adjusted returns, and the positive first year holds only 'once large returns are removed' [S: search summary of Friesen and Swift 2009], which may mean the result depends on trimming. The trade is in every value-investing book (Lynch, Klarman), so the day-5 price may already carry it. Exchange-listed standard conversions are perhaps 2 to 5 a year, so the live book will be near empty and the result may be bank-value beta that KRE does not remove. No post-2009 evidence found.
verdicts.what_would_change_my_mind: Downgrade if the SDC/CRSP count of exchange-listed standard conversions since 2010 is under about 40, if median first-year dollar volume is under $200k a day, or if months 13-30 (the paper's negative window) are not worse than months 1-12 against a matched small-bank basket. The one settling test: day-5 to day-250 less a matched small-bank basket, standard and second-step separately, by era, with the months 13-30 window as the control.

verdicts.name: 2. Insiders buying in their own company's registered offering
verdicts.already_on_desk: Partly. results/ideas/2026-11-15_follow_ons.md: the unconditional rebound is 0.71 gross full sample, 0.26 since 2013, and overnight deals are -0.30 [V: card]. results/ideas/2026-11-12_insider_clusters.md: clusters in the 2,000 largest are 0.05 (t 0.21), and that census explicitly dropped same-price placements, so these events were excluded from the dead test, not tested. The card's reopening condition names 'a narrower event with a mechanism', which this is. A2 (results/events/A2_INSIDER_BUYING_GATE_2026-10-20.md) covers funds only.
verdicts.source_check: Prospectus search re-fetched, HTTP 200: 50 documents for 2025, matching the scout [V]. The Form 4 current-filings feed (sec.gov getcurrent, type=4) returned HTTP 403 to my generic client [V]; SEC wants a declared contact and I supplied none, so I could not confirm it. The desk's own EDGAR client has read sec.gov before, so the endpoint likely works for it [S]. Timing is the real problem: a Form 4 is due two business days after the trade, so entry is D+2 to D+4, on top of or after the desk's measured D+3 to D+7 rebound window. Listed issuers, long-only: tradable in principle.
verdicts.strongest_objection: The names in my own fetch are not officers writing cheques: Biohaven, Kodiak, ProFrac, Hudson Pacific, F&G Annuities [V] are deals where a controlling holder or affiliated fund backstops the offering, which marks a company that could not place the deal without help. verdicts.strongest_objection: Three things can each kill it before a return is read. (1) Size: on the one fund I could size, a 6.5% drop in the underlying gives a forced sale of about 2 x $369m x 6.5% = $48m [arithmetic on V inputs] in a stock that trades billions a day [U]; flagships are near or under the J9 kill line of 1% of volume, and whether any small underlying is materially above it is uncounted. (2) Swaps: the fund's rebalance is a swap reset; the dealer may hedge all afternoon, so the pressure can already be in the 15:45 price the rule buys at. (3) History: CRSP ends 2025-12-31 and most small-underlying funds launched in 2025-26, so the usable sample may be one year of a few dozen names, all in one retail-momentum regime. And the long leg is one-day reversal in small volatile stocks, which the desk already measured as dead since 2013. It also needs a pre-close decision, which the evening pipeline does not have and which paper cannot score properly because paper does not simulate the closing auction.
verdicts.what_would_change_my_mind: It earns TEST_FIRST only because the first step is a count that can end it at zero trials. Run G-J9 re-aimed: for each underlying-day in CRSP 2023-2025, summed L(L-1) x AUM x return over that day's dollar volume. If under 1% on 95% of days with a 5%+ move, kill. If it passes, one pre-set test: close-to-next-open and close-to-next-close return on down-5% days by forced-flow tercile, against (a) the same stock on equally large down days before its fund existed and (b) matched stocks with no fund. The top tercile must beat both controls; equal scores mean it is plain reversal.

verdicts.already_on_desk: Not tested. The closest precedent is C5 (docs/RESEARCH_STATE.md, killed D1): an open-auction fill whose gain turned out to be generic session drift. The ledger line overnight_intraday (results/IDEA_LEDGER.md) is an untested neighbour.
verdicts.source_check: Coinbase's public hourly candle endpoint works without a key: 350 hourly rows, latest 2026-11-16 01:00 UTC [V]. It returns about two weeks per call, so the 2020-2025 history needs paging or another source. Basket list from CoinGecko confirmed (83 .US symbols) [V]. The paper exists (Mourey, Shahrour and Soiman, Finance Research Letters 86, 2025): negative weekend crypto returns predict Monday equity declines, positive ones do not [S, abstract via search; full text not read]. It studies equity indexes, and nothing I could read says the Monday return excludes the opening gap. Stocks and IBIT are tradable at Alpaca; an open entry would need an opening-auction order, which paper does not simulate.
verdicts.strongest_objection: The published effect is almost certainly the gap. These stocks trade pre-market from 04:00 and many overnight, and the spot ETF reprices at the open, so weekend news is in the price before any order the desk can send. The scout's own second source says the gap direction is predictable and that trading it lost money. The rule has no direction ('set by the first test'), which is a search over sign, basket, threshold and window on 10 to 15 large-move weekends a year. The asymmetry in the paper points to the short side, in small miners with uncertain borrow. And the desk's one prior open-fill result died on its placebo.
verdicts.what_would_change_my_mind: The scout's one-afternoon regression, with sign and threshold fixed before looking: Monday open-to-close return of the basket less the coin over the same hours, on the weekend coin return, negative and positive weekends separately. If open-to-close shows nothing and the gap shows everything, close it for good. I would only move if the open-to-close coefficient is significant in both halves of 2020-2025 and absent on a Tuesday-to-Wednesday overnight placebo.
